#9855. As Russia's Cyberwar Evolves, Belarus Steps Forward

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The "FrostyNeighbor" advanced persistent threat (APT) launched a destructive attack in Ukraine and is raising concerns about deeper alignment with Russian cyber objectives.

Researchers have spotted the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor against a critical target in Ukraine, suggesting Belarus may be upping its support for Russian national objectives — carrying implications for much of Europe.

ESET this week published its APT Activity Report for Q2 and Q3 2026. The report highlights a range of state-sponsored activity across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, but one of the most significant assertions involves Belarus, an Eastern European country that has been close allies with Russia in the latter's invasion of Ukraine.

Historically, Belarusian cyber operations have been tracked separately from those attributed directly to Russian intelligence services, though researchers have long observed overlap in targeting and strategic interests. The Belarusan state-affiliated group FrostyNeighbor — also tracked as UNC1151 — has been known for disinformation and cyber espionage, the latter conducted through various means such as spear phishing and malware.

Related:Russia's Hybrid Cyber-Physical War in Europe Heats Up

While the Eastern European country has also set its sights on Ukrainian and Polish targets in phishing attacks to further its own and possibly Russia's goals, ESET identified a recent escalation in these activities. Mainly, ESET's report notes that its researchers "identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater."

Specifically, FrostyNeighbor deployed Chisel, UltraVNC, Cobalt Strike, and a VBScript wiper via Group Policy against a manufacturing company in Ukraine that ESET said "plays an important role in the country's transportation sector," which is notable because destructive operations up until this point have been explicitly Russia-aligned.

"While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia," the report read. "We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas."

Damien Schaeffer, senior malware researcher at ESET, says that the strongest evidence for an increasing operational closeness with Russia is the number of attacks and the victimology that appears closer to and aligned with Russia's strategic priorities than Belarus's own, as well as a sophistication behind these attacks, "which seems relatively high to Belarus's potential interests alone." He says ESET first observed this trend of increasing aggressiveness at the beginning of 2024.

This comes as North Korea expands its own military cooperation with Russia in the latter's war on Ukraine, which ESET added could mean cyber activity will continue to align as well.

Russia's war on Ukraine stretches far beyond Ukraine, especially in the realm of cyber operations. Russia has grown bolder in cyberattacks particularly against European countries that support Ukraine militarily or politically, are on NATO's eastern flank, and support critical logistics hubs for aid flowing into Ukraine.

This, to varying degrees, has included Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Sweden, Czech Republic, and Germany, among others. In other words, if Russian allies are growing bolder in their cyberactivities explicitly supporting Russia, that carries consequences for all of Europe.

Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, tells Dark Reading that its evidence shows FrostyNeighbor as an actor executing sustained operations and evolving its techniques, though not necessarily an overall increase in operational scale nor shared operational command.

Recorded Future's recommendation is to explicitly track Belarus-linked clusters and correlate their infrastructure, tools, and targeting with Russian threat campaigns "while preserving attribution distinctions."

"Threat models should cover credential theft, persistent access, and the use of compromised accounts to reach additional people. Intelligence collection should include malicious login infrastructure, email exploitation, personal-account targeting, and abuse of trusted contacts, which are the access routes documented in these campaigns," Leslie says. "Defenders do not need proof of Russian tasking to prioritize an actor already targeting them."

While researchers differ on whether Belarusian activity represents deeper operational integration with Russia, they appear to agree that defenders should not dismiss Belarus-linked actors as secondary threats. As Leslie explains, CERT Polska in June 2026 identified UNC1151 as one of the most active APT groups it monitors, "observing new phishing domains almost daily in the preceding weeks."

Organizations in sectors tied to government, transportation, and defense that show support for Ukraine may increasingly encounter campaigns whose objectives align closely with Moscow's broader strategic interests.

#9854. Ransomware threat blares from Vanderbilt University computers during cyberattack

BYOD claims extensive data theft as campus Wi-Fi returns, most systems remain restricted, and classes carry on

Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group BYOD.

Vanderbilt announced on Monday morning that it was dealing with "an active cybersecurity incident," and that the fallout may affect university devices, systems, and cloud-based services.

The Nashville-based university initially told students and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi. It warned them to watch for unexpected prompts, altered files or permissions, unfamiliar applications, and unsolicited authentication requests.

Campus computers reportedly began playing an audio threat attributed to BYOD. Student newspaper The Vanderbilt Hustler cited posts on campus social network Fizz showing the message.

"You have been compromised by BYOD," the recording said. "We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one."

By Monday evening, Vanderbilt had restored access to campus Wi-Fi, but warned that access to most systems remains restricted.

"We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university," it said. "Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation."

Students were told to attend classes as scheduled on Tuesday and contact instructors about flexibility on coursework deadlines. Staff were instructed to report to work normally.

Vanderbilt's Athletics department said that its ticketing system was unavailable, and that students were unable to claim tickets for the college's football game against Alabama on Saturday.

BYOD claimed responsibility for the attack on Vanderbilt on Monday, along with extensive data theft.

"If you could not tell already, your databases are locked [and] we have your entire estate and research data," it said via its leak site.

"Over 1 million SSNs, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, student and employee records, full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess."

Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's claims about the extent of its access or the data allegedly stolen.

BYOD may be a familiar name to some. The group previously claimed attacks on the University of New Mexico and Trump Mobile's customer database.

BYOD also claimed responsibility on Monday for an attack on Texas Health and Human Services. The agency has not publicly confirmed an incident and did not immediately respond to our questions. ®

InfoQ Homepage News Cloudflare Develops Public Certificate Authority for Post-Quantum Web Security

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

Cloudflare has tested Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) as an alternative to traditional certificate chains, reporting 9% faster median performance in a Chrome experiment. The approach batches certificate data into an append-only Merkle tree, letting clients verify certificates with compact inclusion proofs instead of transmitting a full certificate chain. Cloudflare attributed most of the measured improvement to eliminating intermediate certificates; the experiment used classical signatures rather than post-quantum signatures.

Building on the approach covered in InfoQ’s earlier report, Cloudflare describes how landmark-based verification and independent transparency log cosigners support certificate issuance and verification at scale.

The experiment served billions of MTCs to 50% of Chrome Beta 146 for selected domains on Cloudflare’s free plan. Cloudflare wound down the experiment in August 2026 and is developing a public certificate authority (CA) that supports MTC issuance, targeting inclusion in Chrome’s quantum-resistant Root Store in early 2027, subject to evaluation.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince, in a press release, said:

Upgrading the web's security before quantum computers can break it is one of the biggest coordination challenges in the history of the Internet.

Post-quantum cryptography creates scaling challenges for the Web Public Key Infrastructure (Web PKI). According to Cloudflare, post-quantum signatures can be approximately 40 times larger than classical signatures, increasing bandwidth and storage requirements.

MTCs combine certificate issuance with transparency logging. Instead of signing certificates individually, a certificate authority (CA) records certificate data in an append-only Merkle tree and signs a checkpoint. Clients verify certificate inclusion using cryptographic proofs.

Cloudflare uses the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol to validate domain ownership. An independent mirroring cosigner verifies and stores updated tree states, helping detect inconsistent log views and preserve issuance records if the original log becomes unavailable.

MTC issuance and independent log mirroring (Source: Cloudflare Blog Post)

Landmark relative certificates further reduce TLS handshake data. Cloudflare distributes authenticated landmarks to clients, which verify certificate inclusion using cryptographic proofs. Servers must still prove possession of their private keys. In the common case, the handshake transmits one public key, one signature, and an inclusion proof smaller than 1 KB.

Landmark relative certificate verification using pre-distributed tree landmarks. (Source: Cloudflare Blog Post)

Clients may be newly installed, offline, or missing the relevant landmark update. Servers must therefore retain a standalone MTC certificate as a fallback. Cloudflare identifies independent monitoring at production volume, a diverse ecosystem of CAs and cosigners, and browser support as remaining requirements for broader deployment. Alicja Tendaj, Tier 2 Technical Support Specialist at SSL.com, raised questions about revocation and incident handling in response to Cloudflare’s announcement on LinkedIn:

With short validity and trust anchored in a tree head, a lot of the old OCSP and CRL playbook becomes a question of how quickly you can stop including a certificate

Cloudflare’s planned public CA will require evaluation before its MTC issuance can be trusted through Chrome’s quantum-resistant Root Store. The company says production deployment will help determine whether the approach can maintain transparency, interoperability, and availability at Internet scale.

#9852. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister."

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to new audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

#9851. Chrome zero-day whack-a-mole continues as 2026 tally hits 8

Another Chrome memory bug gets squashed, but not before attackers got their hands on it

Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar.

The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted.

"Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks.

The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited.

Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit.

The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine.

The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited.

The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight.

That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess.

Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

#9850. Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

A security firm patched a decade-old app to prevent the takeover of millions of machines, highlighting that abandoned domains remain a boon to attackers.

When managed security service provider Eye Security spotted an odd update process in a client's telemetry that appeared to be reaching out to outdated — and in some cases, malicious — domains, the company decided to take a deeper look.

The updater belonged to a modified version of Time4Popcorn, a 2014-era BitTorrent client that allows movies to be downloaded from the Internet, and even after a decade, the persistent updater continued to run on more than 2.5 million Windows machines and an estimated 300,000 Macs, checking for new software, according to the MSSP's advisory. The problem: Many of the domains checked by the updater were open to registration, which could allow any would-be cyberattacker to register the domain and have an easy way to place software on millions of machines.

The situation highlights the issue of old infrastructure and the threat it poses to users and businesses, especially if the business's employees work from home, Niels Teusink, principal security researcher for Eye Security, wrote in the analysis.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

"[W]hile these users chose to install Popcorn Time, none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years, ready to run any code with full privileges for whoever controlled one of its domains," the company stated in its advisory. "With millions of systems affected and the software long abandoned, there was no vendor to fix this and no patch on the way: if we didn't act, nobody would."

The risk of domains that are dropped by a legitimate service and then picked up again, or bought by a gray-market or criminal operator — sometimes called "dropcatch domains" — have become an increasing issue as developers have stopped updating, or sold off, legacy software infrastructure. In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million HTTP requests from government and companies came in for resources that had been hosted at those addresses.

And with AI enabling a more sophisticated analysis of software projects, attackers may be able to more quickly do the necessary research to find domains that could be a backdoor into users' systems, says Benjamin Harris, founder and CEO of watchTowr.

"AI is definitely driving the barrier-to-entry down for this kind of research very quickly," he says. "We're seeing AI used to reproduce vulnerabilities, find zero days, but applied to this, AI can be used to install a bunch of software, install network taps, see what all the software reaches out to, see what's not registered, or see what's been abandoned and what we can hijack."

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

Typically, there are two types of vulnerable domains that questionable operators might take an interest in. The first are homograph domains that look like their legitimate cousins and include both typosquatting domains, such as "gmai[.]com," that try to catch browsers whose users mistyped a URL, and lookalike domains that are used in phishing to visually fool users. The value of these types of domains to the owner varies, depending on the amount of traffic they attract, says Renée Burton, vice president of threat intelligence at cybersecurity vendor Infoblox.

However, dropcatch domains that are integrated into the supply chain for a piece of software are a completely different — and more serious — risk, she says. Infoblox has registered hundreds of domains that had been part of supply chains to prevent attackers from using them.

"Supply chain attacks can happen at a moment's notice, and depending on how dropped domains are integrated into existing software, a threat actor can quickly abuse a supply chain dropped domain to conduct sophisticated attacks that lead to data loss and ransomware," Burton says.

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

In 2024, Chinese company Funnull bought the polyfill[.]io domain from the creator of the Polyfill service and began redirecting users to tens of thousands of websites.

The Popcorn Time issue highlights the problem. Anyone with access to the domains, and with some reverse engineering, could figure out how to tinker with the legacy updaters. In fact, that's what Eye Security did, updating the code to stop the automated process of reaching out to the old domains.

"All we needed to do was supply a link to an executable and the program would download it and then execute it with high privileges (NT AUTHORITYSYSTEM)," Teusink wrote. "There was no code signing and this process was all happening over HTTP."

Eye Security stressed that another project, confusingly also named Popcorn Time, is a 2025 effort to create a legitimate streaming service and is not impacted by the legacy update issues.

Companies should know the domains that their employees are reaching out to and the reputation of those domains, and should extend that monitoring and protection to remote users, says watchTowr's Harris.

"The big challenge with things like BYOD and working from home is that now the network perimeter extends from not just your corporate network ... but the user's home network as well," he says.

The community needs to come together as well, says Infoblox's Burton. While taking active defense to the same extent as Eye Security continues to be legally problematic, finding legacy and unused infrastructure is something that security communities on the Internet can continue to work on, she says.

"Threat actors understand the value of controlling a domain which is integrated into an existing supply chain and being queried by real people on a regular basis," Burton says. "We need more defenders looking for proactive ways to disrupt domain drop schemes by purchasing high-value pending drop domains before threat actors, and by looking for ways to reduce threat actors cash out opportunities from these attacks."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9849. Memory Safety Bugs in Rust Standard Library

By Yechan Bae / November 9, 2026 / 19 min read

Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent.

Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly important as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate.

Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today.

In this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. We use them to discuss what Rust does and doesn’t guarantee, why writing correct unsafe Rust is so difficult, and why Rust’s safety model still matters even though its memory safety isn’t perfect.

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we study vulnerabilities in complex software, including the Rust standard library. Our team combines years of experience in vulnerability research with AI-assisted tools that help us investigate code and find bugs that are difficult to uncover through traditional analysis alone.

Some of the bugs in this post were found with help from Hyenas, our research version of codename MDASH. Our researchers investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed their potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them.

This post focuses on soundness bugs in the standard library’s unsafe code. Bugs in the compiler itself, such as miscompilations and holes in the type system, are a different topic that we don’t cover here.

A note on open issues. At publication, two of the issues reported by our team remain open. The article also references related issues reported by others and fixes that are still under review. The Rust maintainers triaged and responded to our reports quickly, and we believe maintainers and the contributors working on these issues are doing their best and making the right tradeoffs among the many bugs they handle.

If you’re interested in an open issue, please comment only when you have something genuinely new to contribute, such as new information or an affected real-world use case.

At the lowest level, Rust uses unsafe blocks to work with raw pointers and interact directly with the operating system. Much of the standard library, including Vec and String, is built from small unsafe pieces wrapped in safe APIs. Inside an unsafe block, the programmer takes responsibility for the guarantees the compiler can’t check, and that responsibility extends to the safe API built around it. That API must be sound: no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.

Upholding that promise is harder than it looks. Consider a function that returns the byte at idx from any type that can be viewed as a byte slice, skipping the redundant bounds check after doing its own:

The hard part of unsafe Rust is knowing what you can trust. The function above looks correct, but it assumes that two calls to as_ref return the same slice. Because S is chosen by the caller, a safe AsRef implementation can return a long slice the first time and an empty one the second, and get reads out of bounds. Unsafe code must be careful with every call it makes, and the bugs we found fall into three patterns of misplaced trust: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Unsafe code often breaks an invariant for a moment and restores it afterward; for example, it may allocate an uninitialized buffer and fill it directly, avoiding redundant writes to zero the memory first. That’s fine as long as the function runs to the end. But many operations in Rust can panic, from out-of-bounds indexing to calls into user-provided code, and by default a panic unwinds: it leaves the function early while still running destructors. Unwinding inside that window becomes an invisible exit that exposes the broken invariant to code that trusts it. Bugs of this kind are called panic safety bugs.

We identified a panic safety issue in MapWindows::clone. Iterator::map_windows, a nightly API, yields overlapping windows of N items. It keeps the current window in a Buffer whose destructor drops the N items starting at start. In Rust 1.97.0, library/core/src/iter/adapters/map_windows.rs defines it as:

Buffer::clone, in the same file, built the new buffer first and filled it afterward:

After line 197, buffer breaks its own invariant: its slots are uninitialized, but its destructor is already armed. The clone() call on line 201 runs the user’s T::clone before the slots are written. If that call panics, unwinding drops buffer and runs drop_in_place on N uninitialized values. Our proof of concept uses only safe code: an element type whose clone always panics, which causes a crash when the destructor accesses uninitialized memory. The fix holds the new buffer in ManuallyDrop until it is fully written, so unwinding leaks the half-built buffer instead of dropping it.

The general lesson is to treat every call to code you don’t control, such as clone, drop, comparisons, closures, and iterator methods, as a possible early exit. Either finish the work that may panic before breaking an invariant, or make the broken state safe to unwind through: hold it in ManuallyDrop, or use a guard whose destructor restores the invariant, like Vec’s internal SetLenOnDrop. The Rustonomicon covers this under exception safety.

The recently stabilized Allocator API shows how hard panic safety is to get right. With std, an allocation failure aborts the process by default instead of unwinding, so much of the standard library’s unsafe code assumes allocation never unwinds. Custom allocators can break that assumption. While the API was being stabilized, we reported one place in BTreeMap::insert that becomes unsound when an allocator unwinds, and others reported more (#159334, #159368, #159370). Fixing them one by one would mean auditing everything that allocates, so the stabilization, shipping in Rust 1.100 on November 12, instead requires implementors never to unwind from the trait’s methods or from drop. The proposal notes that “unwinding out of many allocation-related methods was found to be a pervasive source of unsoundness.”

Unsafe code often calls into code its caller provides: a comparator, a trait implementation, a closure. That code is safe, but safe doesn’t mean correct, and it can return inconsistent or plainly wrong answers. The question is who is responsible when it does. In C++, it’s the caller. std::sort requires its comparator to be a strict weak ordering, and breaking that rule is undefined behavior. With libstdc++, sorting equal elements with <= reads past the end of the vector:

The same comparator passed to Rust’s sort_by is only a logic error. The sort may panic or leave the slice in an unspecified order, but it never causes undefined behavior. The responsibility sits with the unsafe code. The comparator is safe code supplied by the caller, so the unsafe code inside the sort must stay sound no matter what it returns. The same goes for every safe trait a user can implement: comparisons can be inconsistent, an ExactSizeIterator can report a length that doesn’t match the items it yields, and Borrow can return a different value on each call.

Another of our bug reports shows how easy this trust is to miss: str::replace with a custom Pattern can create a non-UTF-8 String. String search APIs accept any type that implements the nightly Pattern trait, and a pattern can describe itself through as_utf8_pattern. str::replace uses that description to take a fast path when replacing one ASCII byte with another. In Rust 1.96.0, the fast path in library/alloc/src/str.rs looked like this:

replace_ascii, in the same file, then rewrites the bytes:

The CharPattern branch on line 272 checks that the character is ASCII, but the StringPattern branch on line 271 assumes a one-byte string pattern must be ASCII. That holds for &str patterns, but StringPattern stored &[u8], and as_utf8_pattern is a safe method any Pattern can implement. In our proof of concept, a custom pattern reports the single byte 0x80, which only appears inside multibyte UTF-8 sequences:

str::replace rewrites the continuation bytes and returns a String that isn’t valid UTF-8, and later string operations that rely on UTF-8 reach undefined behavior. The fix changed StringPattern to hold &str instead of &[u8], so the type itself now guarantees UTF-8.

When unsafe code depends on a property of a user-provided implementation, don’t take it on faith. Call the implementation once and keep the result, validate what it returns, or encode the property in a type that safe code can’t forge, as this fix did. If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it.

join shows how easy it is to fix this kind of bug only partway. In 2020, we reported that it trusted Borrow::borrow to return the same string on each call (CVE-2020-36323), and the fix handled strings that shrink between calls. In April 2026, the same function needed another fix: join borrows the first element twice, and if it grows on the second call, the remaining-length calculation underflows into a heap overflow. The earlier fix had never covered that path.

Others reported similar problems in the Pattern API this year. A safe Pattern can hand back a valid searcher built for a different string, and consumers such as strip_prefix_of apply its ranges to the original string unchecked, reading out of bounds (#158265). The same problem turned up in split_once (#165076) after a report that the Searcher contract doesn’t spell out what str::split relies on (#164904). Both bugs are still open.

The first two patterns stay inside Rust code. The third sits at the boundary with the operating system, where unsafe code trusts process-wide state such as signal stacks, memory mappings, and the environment, which other threads, C libraries, or the kernel can touch at any time. These bugs have been hard to find automatically, because a static analyzer would need to model all of that surrounding behavior. AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search. We started exploring it and found some interesting bugs.

When a thread overflows its stack, Rust prints a clear message and aborts instead of crashing with a bare segmentation fault:

This relies on a few pieces of process-wide state. Each thread’s stack ends in a guard page, an inaccessible region just past the stack’s limit: pthread reserves one for every spawned thread, and on Linux the kernel’s own stack guard plays that role for the main thread. Touching it raises SIGSEGV, and Rust registers a handler for that signal. The handler can’t run on the stack that just overflowed, so Rust also gives each thread an alternate signal stack, a small separate mapping with a guard page of its own, which the kernel switches to when it delivers the signal. The handler checks that the faulting address is inside the guard page, prints the message, and aborts.

We found that calling process::exit from a child thread tears down the main thread’s alternate stack while the main thread is still running. process::exit runs the runtime’s cleanup before calling libc’s exit, and in Rust 1.98.0 that cleanup ends in library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs:

Line 202 passes MAIN_ALTSTACK, the main thread’s alternate stack, to drop_handler:

Line 298 disables the alternate stack of the calling thread, but line 301 unmaps the main thread’s. The code assumes it runs on the main thread, which isn’t true when a child thread calls process::exit. The main thread keeps running until libc’s exit finishes, with its signal stack registration still pointing at unmapped memory. If it overflows its stack in that window, the kernel can’t deliver the signal, and our proof of concept dies with a plain segmentation fault instead of Rust’s message. The bug dates back to 2015, and the fix stops cleaning up the main thread’s alternate stack altogether.

We also checked whether this could become a security issue. In theory, it could lead to code execution: if a writable mapping landed at the old alternate stack’s address, the kernel would deliver the main thread’s next signal onto it, and another thread could overwrite the handler’s frame, such as its return address, while it runs. In practice, the conditions are very tight. Everything has to happen in the brief window before libc’s exit finishes, the new mapping must have exactly the right size to reuse that address, and overwriting the frame takes a second race inside a short handler. For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. This assessment does not automatically apply to the other issues discussed. The issue has more details in its security impact analysis.

Our other report involves the process environment. On Unix, CommandExt::exec replaces the current process with a new program. When the command has its own environment variables, exec points the process-global environ at a new array, calls execvp, and restores environ if execvp fails. In Rust 1.99.0, Command::exec takes the environment lock in library/std/src/sys/process/unix/unix.rs:

Command::do_exec, in the same file, then swaps the environment:

Line 242 takes only the read side of the environment lock, yet line 410 writes the process-global environ; line 409 saves the old value so it can be restored if execvp on line 413 fails. Writing environ under a read lock lets other threads in. A thread calling env::var takes the same read lock and can see variables meant only for the new program, and two failed exec calls racing each other can leave environ pointing at a freed array that a later env::vars_os() reads. Both proofs of concept use only safe Rust. A 2018 fix held an exclusive lock here, but when the environment lock became a read-write lock in 2021, exec kept the read side. A fix that avoids touching environ by calling execve directly is in review.

The environment has caused trouble before. After a discussion that began in 2015, the 2024 edition marked env::set_var as unsafe, because C functions on most Unix platforms read the environment without going through Rust’s lock.

Getting this boundary right is hard, and more problems are still open. While exploring this area, we independently ran into a double free in safe code that process::exit can cause through thread-local destructors. It was reported by someone else (#164243), but it’s worth mentioning here. libc’s exit first runs the calling thread’s thread-local destructors, as C++ requires, and Rust registers its destructors the same way. If a destructor calls process::exit while a thread local is being replaced, libc drops that thread local a second time. A proposed fix switches process::exit to POSIX _exit, which ends the process without running these handlers.

Every unsafe block rests on assumptions about the code around it. The bugs in this post came from three kinds of misplaced trust:

The first two patterns are well studied. Rudra looked for both in 2021, and the standard library was already fixing panic safety bugs in 2015 (CVE-2015-20001). They remain challenging to avoid because any call inside unsafe code might unwind or run code the caller supplied.

What we saw this year was mixed. On the positive side, the nightly process is working. Many reports were caught while the affected APIs were still unstable, and several were fixed by changing the design before stabilization. StringPattern now holds &str instead of &[u8], and Allocator was stabilized with a rule that implementors must not unwind. At the same time, bugs in these patterns still reach stable releases, and their fixes aren’t always complete. join was fixed in 2020 and needed another fix in 2026 for a path the first fix had missed.

The third pattern is different. Its bugs live where Rust meets the layers below it: the kernel, through system calls such as sigaltstack and munmap, and the C library, through process-wide state such as environ and the cleanup that libc’s exit runs. Getting them right takes knowledge that lives outside Rust’s type system, which has made these bugs difficult to find with traditional static analysis. That may also be why they last so long. The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years, and exec has written environ under a read lock since 2021. Unlike our reports in the first two patterns, both affect stable Rust.

Language models already know a great deal about how these interfaces behave, so agentic scanners can check unsafe code against the system it runs on, not just the language. We think this boundary is one of the most promising places for agentic security research, in Rust and beyond.

Rust holds its safe APIs to a stricter standard than C and C++. Safe code must never be able to cause undefined behavior, no matter how it uses an API. In C++, a comparator that breaks std::sort’s ordering requirement causes undefined behavior, while Rust’s sort must stay memory-safe with any Ord implementation. POSIX doesn’t guarantee that setenv is safe to call while another thread reads the environment. That makes memory safety bugs in Rust hard to compare one-to-one with bugs in other languages.

For the same reason, a soundness bug in the standard library isn’t automatically a vulnerability in the programs that use it. Each bug in this post needs an unusual setup to trigger, such as a panic at exactly the wrong moment, a deliberately misbehaving implementation, or calling process::exit from a child thread. It becomes a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way.

Rust’s safety standard is strict and difficult to meet, but it’s also useful. It gives an unambiguous answer to what counts as a soundness bug, so problems can be fixed and prevented once in the library, instead of in every program that uses it. Rust’s safety model strikes the right balance between control, safety, and performance for systems programming, which is why so many projects choose it.

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re exploring how technology such as codename MDASH can help researchers find bugs like the ones in this post at greater scale. Rust’s standard library is one of several foundational open source projects where we’re applying this approach.

This research also extends beyond the lab. It helps inform the development of codename MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. These findings can also serve as inputs to Microsoft Perception, our new multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work together across broader security workflows. For example, the Web App Pen Test Agent can use codename MDASH findings to help prioritize testing, validate exploitability against live applications, and produce actionable vulnerabilities that downstream agents can use to prioritize and support remediation. This connects AI-powered code analysis with real-world security validation and response, helping security teams move from identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding and addressing actual risk.

Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs, it’s to identify meaningful issues, turn those findings into actionable research, and improve the safety of foundational software that developers and organizations depend on.

#9848. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

The lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

#9847. L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

I ricercatori non riescono a spiegare del tutto perché le minacce informatiche in Italia siano così diverse rispetto a quelle di qualsiasi altro Paese.

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

Secondo nuovi dati, l’Italia è vittima di un numero sproporzionatamente elevato di attacchi informatici. Non solo: le tipologie di attacchi che colpiscono le organizzazioni nel Paese sono molto diverse da quelle che colpiscono altre località. I ricercatori avanzano tre teorie per spiegarne il motivo.

È vero che alcune regioni e alcuni paesi sono esposti a un rischio informatico maggiore a causa di fattori economici, militari e politici. Israele è una calamita per gli hacktivisti e per le minacce persistenti avanzate (APT) regionali, legate agli Stati. La storia unica del Brasile lo rende un vero e proprio alveare di trojan bancari. L’economia degli Stati Uniti attirerà sempre la massima attenzione da parte dei truffatori. Non è però così ovvio il motivo per cui l’Italia sia un bersaglio così popolare per i criminali informatici.

Related:Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

«Uno dei motivi principali per cui abbiamo deciso di esaminare il panorama delle minacce in Italia è che il Paese continuava a comparire in cima alle nostre statistiche nei rapporti interni mensili», afferma Gianluca Tiepolo, analista di criminalità informatica presso Intel471. In un rapporto condiviso in esclusiva con Dark Reading prima della sua pubblicazione, Intel471 ha rilevato che l’Italia rappresenta un vero e proprio caso a sé stante nel panorama globale delle minacce informatiche. Le organizzazioni italiane subiscono attacchi a un ritmo ben superiore a quanto ci si potrebbe ragionevolmente aspettare, considerando le dimensioni del Paese, la sua economia e la sua situazione politica. Inoltre, gli attacchi sfruttanti le vulnerabilità e le infrastrutture web sono molto più comuni in Italia che altrove.

«Volevamo capire cosa fosse alla base di quelle statistiche», afferma Tiepolo. Alla fine, però, i dati dipingono un quadro quasi inspiegabile di ciò che sta accadendo nella terra della pasta e del Chianti.

L’Italia è il 25° Paese più grande al mondo ma, secondo questi nuovi dati, le sue organizzazioni rappresentano circa il 7% di tutti i dati di accesso iniziale venduti sui forum dei criminali informatici. A livello globale, è seconda solo agli Stati Uniti (30%). L’Italia si colloca inoltre al quarto posto tra i Paesi più presi di mira dal ransomware.

Ancora più strani sono i tipi di intrusioni informatiche che colpiscono le organizzazioni in Italia. Secondo i nuovi dati, gli initial access broker (IAB) hanno ottenuto il loro primo punto d’appoggio sfruttando vulnerabilità nel 57% dei casi. Le credenziali hanno spiegato solo il 23% dei casi. Nel frattempo, gli IAB hanno venduto l’accesso all’infrastruttura web di proprietà delle vittime nel 49% dei casi, con strumenti di accesso remoto e desktop remoto che rappresentano il 26% dei casi.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

E allora? Forse queste cifre non saltano all’occhio. Ora, però, confrontiamole con i dati di Intel471 tratti dal suo rapporto “2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook”:

A livello globale nel 2025, gli IAB hanno preso di mira gli strumenti di accesso remoto e di desktop remoto nel 67% dei casi — il 41% in più, in termini relativi, rispetto all’Italia. Nel frattempo, l’infrastruttura web — di gran lunga la risorsa più a rischio in Italia — rappresentava una frazione talmente esigua dei dati globali di Intel471 che l’azienda non si è nemmeno preoccupata di citarla nel proprio rapporto.

Allo stesso modo, secondo i dati globali dell’azienda, gli attacchi basati sulle credenziali sono oggi, in generale, otto volte più comuni di qualsiasi altro tipo di attacco. È emerso che il 49% delle inserzioni su IAB indicava le credenziali come tipo di attacco, rispetto al 23% dei dati specifici per l’Italia. E, cosa davvero esilarante, mentre in Italia rappresentano circa il 57% di tutti gli attacchi, le vulnerabilità sfruttate sono emerse solo nel 6,5% dei casi a livello globale.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Sebbene i dati sulla sicurezza informatica possano essere interpretati in modi diversi a seconda delle circostanze, l’Italia sembra davvero una sorta di “unicorno” del rischio informatico, afferma Tiepolo, aggiungendo che l’Italia è ormai da tempo in ritardo in termini di preparazione informatica.

«Sono italiano», dice. «Ho lavorato con molti clienti italiani diversi. Quello che posso dire è che l’Italia è probabilmente leggermente indietro rispetto ad altri paesi europei, semplicemente in termini di [adozione delle] tecnologie di sicurezza. Ad esempio, le tecnologie di rilevamento e risposta sugli endpoint (EDR) sono diventate popolari in Italia intorno al 2020–2021. Prima del 2020, la maggior parte delle aziende italiane non utilizzava la tecnologia EDR. Quindi, forse storicamente, l’Italia è un po’ indietro nell’investire effettivamente in prodotti e tecnologie di sicurezza informatica».

Inoltre, i criminali informatici opportunisti stanno sfruttando in massa vulnerabilità note, diffuse e spesso piuttosto datate per mietere un numero maggiore di vittime in Italia rispetto ad altri paesi. «I dati che abbiamo visto la scorsa settimana da PHP2Shell, credo, confermano questa valutazione. L’Italia è il paese europeo con il maggior numero di versioni PHP 4, 5 e 7, che sono ormai fuori supporto», osserva Tiepolo.

«Ben il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale rivolte all’Italia sono quelle che chiamiamo “offerte all’ingrosso”», ipotizza. «Non si tratta di offerte mirate specificatamente all’Italia, ma semplicemente di sfruttamento delle vulnerabilità. La nostra valutazione è che l’Italia sia probabilmente più lenta di altri paesi nell’applicare le patch ai propri sistemi».

Un’altra possibilità correlata è che l’Italia si trovi vittima di una sorta di effetto rete delle vulnerabilità informatiche. La logica è più o meno questa: se determinate tecnologie sono particolarmente diffuse in un paese come l’Italia e le organizzazioni sono lente nell’affrontare le vulnerabilità di tali tecnologie, allora quel paese diventa un’economia di scala attraente.

Come ha scritto Intel471 nel proprio rapporto: «Una volta che un attore sviluppa un metodo di sfruttamento efficace, può applicare tale metodo ad altri sistemi esposti senza dover condurre un’attività di ricognizione separata ed estesa contro ciascuna organizzazione. Ciò riduce lo sforzo necessario per compromettere aziende la cui dimensione o il cui profilo potrebbero altrimenti offrire un incentivo limitato per un’intrusione mirata».

I ricercatori non hanno potuto specificare esattamente a quali tecnologie, vulnerabilità o metodi di sfruttamento questa teoria possa riferirsi, ma hanno osservato che essa si inserisce nel dato secondo cui il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale alle organizzazioni italiane online viene venduto all’ingrosso.

Senza avallare specificatamente i dati o le conclusioni di Intel471, i rappresentanti della società di sicurezza informatica Cleafy, con sede a Milano, hanno dichiarato a Dark Reading di aver osservato modelli sostanzialmente simili.

«La nostra ricerca sulle minacce evidenzia effettivamente un modello correlato: gli autori degli attacchi riutilizzano strumenti, infrastrutture e tecniche per estendere le campagne a diversi obiettivi bancari italiani», ha scritto l’azienda via e-mail. Ha citato casi come il kit di iniezione web drIBAN, che gli autori degli attacchi hanno utilizzato per sfruttare il sistema di Posta Elettronica Certificata (PEC), ampiamente diffuso in Italia. Casi come quello di drIBAN «non dimostrano che l’Italia abbia un mercato di accesso iniziale sproporzionatamente ampio, ma illustrano come le tecniche di attacco e le infrastrutture riutilizzabili possano aiutare i criminali informatici a estendere le operazioni su più obiettivi».

C’è un altro fattore, potenzialmente significativo, che spiega perché l’Italia appaia così diversa dagli altri paesi nei set di dati sugli attacchi informatici: la prevalenza delle piccole imprese.

La maggior parte delle imprese, ovunque, è di piccole dimensioni, ma, almeno rispetto ad altre economie avanzate, ciò è particolarmente vero in Italia. Una “panoramica dei dati per l’Italia” del maggio 2024 redatta da McKinsey ha rilevato che le “MSME” — micro, piccole e medie imprese — hanno contribuito all’economia e all’occupazione italiane in misura superiore di circa il 10% rispetto alla loro quota relativa in altre economie avanzate. Lo scorso marzo, inoltre, l’Organizzazione per la cooperazione e lo sviluppo economico (OCSE) ha pubblicato un rapporto in cui si indicava che nel 2023 il 99,9% delle imprese italiane era costituito da PMI e il 94,8% da microimprese.

«L’Italia ha molte piccole e medie imprese», afferma Tiepolo. «Una delle cose emerse dai dati — in particolare quelli relativi alle estorsioni — è che questi gruppi prendono di mira [in modo sproporzionato] le piccole e medie imprese. Quindi questo potrebbe essere uno dei motivi per cui [l’Italia si distingue] rispetto ad altri paesi che hanno un maggior numero di grandi aziende».

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
