#9811. Building a networking switch ASIC chip

I am currently on a quest to build some open source networking equipment with the final boss being a full router.

There are a lot of very valuable and less complex pieces of hardware on the way that also need building, one of them being the common networking switch.

Previously I was building the infrastructure to handle ethernet packets and worked my way up to a simple three-port switch that I had taped it out via Tiny Tapeout. But a few days after that tapeout, as I was still reeling from the adrenaline of rushing to meet the deadline, an unexpected opportunity presented itself: the possibility of taping out my own full chip, free of charge!

But there was one slight problem, I only had four days to design the entire thing, also known as 96 hours ( putting it in hours definitely does not make it sound less terrifying ).

A few months back, I wrote that building a full matrix multiplication accelerator with some in-silicon debug infrastructure in under 2 weeks was too tight of a deadline, all around a terrible idea and should absolutely never be attempted, especially not in a corporate setting. Well since then I have discovered a new circle of hell: designing a full ASIC solo in 4 days.

But now that I have gazed upon these new depths of hell, let me tell you about the journey of building full ASICs!

Fully open-source full chip tapeout of the unmanaged cut-through 100Mbps Ethernet switch and the Heat Death of the Universe beacon. Targeting 0.5x0.5 waffer.space run#2.

But they will talk to wafer.space, and wafer.space will talk to me.

Now I suspect you might be wondering: what is wafer.space again ?

A few months ago, something happened. Tim Ansell, formerly part of the team at Google that got us the SkyWater 130nm and GlobalFoundries 180nm open source PDKs, left Google and started wafer.space where he opened up the possibility for mere mortals to taped out their own chip at GlobalFoundries for an affordable price. They offer the services of getting your chip manufactured on GlobalFoundaries 180nm and optionally get it packaged.

Chips come in all rectangular sizes with the size measured in area.

Area is one of the primary concerns of the design as it is once again a question of cold calculated economics, because, when you go to get a chip manufactured you pay per \( mm^2 \) of area.

Take for example the price quoted bellow by IHP (another fab) for their own multiwafer runs. If you participate in this run you will get back a set number of chips (40 in this case) and your final chip cost will correspond to how big your chip ultimately is.

Yet, more area is not simply more expensive because of the direct manufacturing cost, there is a second more subtle factor inflating the price, and that is yield.

Ultimately broken chips have no value, actually we could argue that we should ascribe negative value to broken chips because identifying which chips are broken costs money, and selling a customer a broken chip costs even more money. So maximizing the ratio of good chips to manufactured chips is of primary importance. This ratio is called the yield.

Chips can be broken for a plethora of reasons, but for simplicity I will put them in two different buckets. Firstly it could be a design issue, in which case all your chips are equally affected. Secondly it could be a manufacturing defect that affects your chips semi-randomly.

Manufacturing defects that occur during semiconductor device fabrication can be modeled as constant defect probability per unit of area, meaning that chips with higher area have a higher probability of having a defect, and thus lower yield, leading to ultimately higher costs.

This doesn’t impact the price which I pay to the chip area per-se, but it affects the average net price that I will pay per functional chip.

This is the double reason why area optimization is such a concern when designing chips.

Now GlobaFoundaries 180nm (gf180) is not a young node, and the polite way of calling something old is “mature”. With node maturity comes increased expertise of the process by the foundry leading to better yields over time. So gf180 is a node with excellent yields for which area related defects are not a concern especially compared to younger leading edge nodes.

Wafer.space now offers 4 chip sizes, commonly referred to in the community as the “full”, “half”s and “quarter” slots.

For people in need of some perspective, the full slot and its nearly 13mm2 of area is the same size as the entire Tiny Tapeout gf180 shuttle chip. The same chip that is capable of accommodating unto 160 project tiles and all the Tiny Tapeout common infrastructure. For reference, my two systolic arrays (8 bit integer and bfloat16) and the original switch all fit on only 4 tiles and my largest design to date, the blake2s hashing accelerator on 8.

But getting the silicon manufactured is only the first battle of the war.

Once you get your chip onto a wafer, there are two more important steps to clear before it can actually be called a chip.

Semiconductors are manufactured on a substrate called a wafer, this is a solid silicon disk that then needs to be very precisely broken up into individual chips. This step is called dicing.

So once the wafers have exited the fab and the guys at wafer.space take delivery of the full set of wafers, they call to another specialized service to dice them into individual chips along the scrible lines using a very precise diamond saw.

At that point, wafer.space offers two possibilities. The first is to mail you the diced chips directly, the second is to get the chips packaged for you.

Raw semiconductor silicon is beautiful but unless you are also in the habit of collecting expensive crystals to look at, they are not much use as is. After all, how do you communicate with a piece of doped silicon crystal?

In order to both power our chip and be able to communicate with it, we need to package it in the form in which we can connect it to a wider electronic circuit.

That is, unless you just happen to have a micromanipulator and about 56 microprobes lying in your garage that you can use for chip bringup. In which case please do tell me if you ever need some help clearing out your garage, I have nothing planned that day.

Chip packages come in different forms, the most common being some kind of black plastic enclosures used not only to create accessible connections to the silicon but also for protecting the delicate die and the connections from the environmental damage caused by shocks, humidity and extreme temperature fluctuations.

The type of package we chose also affects how we architect the IO and thus what our silicon floorplan will look like. There are two big families of packages:

In the case of flip-chips the IO pin connections will be spread out regularly all over the floorplan leading to shorter logic to pin connections, and supporting a greater pin density and count. But on the flip side (put intended), flip chips packaging requires a lot more precision and is more expensive compared to …

Wire bonding works by conning your silicon to a pad in the package using a very thin fly wire made from gold or aluminium.

This is done by a wire bonding machine that will physically pull a wire from a IO landing pad on the silicon and connect it to a landing pad on the package. The silicon would be placed at the center of the package and would be connected to the pads placed all around it on the package, themselves connected to the larger exterior pads.

In this case the IO pad structures of the silicon would be located towards the exterior of the chip creating two distinct zones, the padring and the core region where most of the logic is located.

There are many sub-flavors of wire bonded packaging, and wafer.space decided to offer something called chip-on-board packaging (CoB), which is a bit different to how mass market chips are classically packaged but also much more cost effective for small scale fabrication.

For CoB the chip is not bonded out to an enclosed package, but rather, the connections are made directly to a PCB.

Once the chip has been bonded onto the PCB, a protective epoxy layer called a globtop is deposited and hardened on top of the silicon and the bonds. Some of you might have already noticed black blobs on commercial PCBs in the past, and without even realizing it you might have been looking at a CoB packaging.

But unlike the dull black glob tops, wafer.space has opted for the rarer beautifully transparent epoxy, allowing you to directly see the chip bonded though the package.

With your silicon bonded you now have what can officially be called a chip! 🥳

What wafer.space is selling : the possibility for anyone to make their own full prototype chip run for the price of an expensive vacation, is honestly revolutionary.

DARPA and google gave us the tools, Tiny Tapeout offered us a chance to sharpen our skills and wafer.space gave us direct access to manufacturing.

Once more, in the spirit of transparency, I was invited onto the shuttle for free, but this sentiment comes from a genuine belief, so much so that as soon as the following manufacturing run sales opened I put my money where my mouth is, and bought my slot outright.

Somehow this is still cheaper than flying back for Christmas.

If you are new here and this is your first time reading this blog, welcome.

For those for whom this isn’t our first rodeo: you might be wondering how full chips differ from what I have been doing so far ?

In previous episodes, I had been taping out my designs through Tiny Tapeout. Tiny Tapeout is a shuttle chip where multiple projects share the same chip, and in doing so share a common infrastructure. That infrastructure includes handling the silicon’s IO, the power and clock distribution as well as manufacturing and sticking the chip onto a functional development boards.

All important parts that I now get the luxury of handling on my own, which also means I also get the luxury of making all the mistakes!

But, after having gotten the chance to perfect my understanding and experience of the tapeout process through 9 prior Tiny Tapeout tapeouts this sounds the natural next step.

With Tiny Tapeout, you don’t control the number of pins, nor do you have a precise idea of the timing of the signals arriving from the chip’s pins to the pins of your macro. Additionally, even though you can buy extra tiles on Tiny Tapeout, the smallest quarter slot chip on wafer.space still gives you more core area than the largest configuration of Tiny Tapeout has to offer. And finally, Tiny Tapeout only gives you one chip per dev board, whereas with wafer.space you get a minimum order lot size of 1000 chips.

For the purposes of the networking chip project, the real game changer is having control over the pin architecture, meaning I can now decide both the number and the type of the pins.

Because I am comunicating with the PHY chip using an RMII interface, I care very much about pins as each Ethernet port interface requires 7 pins. This was also the reason why the initial version of the networking switch had only 3 ports: I only had 24 pins.

You can refer to the previous article Designing an Ethernet Switch ASIC for an explanation on why each port needs 7 pins and each pin is used for.

So now that I have a whopping 46 pins maximum to play with, we can get cooking!

Anatomically pins are analog blocks with a landing pad for the wire bonded wire on one end. These are included as part of the GlobalFoundries open source foundry provided IO cell library, and although all the pins share the same height, width and landing pad sizes, each features different analog layouts according to its functionality.

The most important types of pins for this design are the input pins, the bidirectional pins and the power delivery pins. Have fun playing spot the difference.

Interestingly, the standard library does not offer any pure output pins, so outputs are handled by bidirectional pins statically configured in output mode.

Looking at the floorplans provided above you might notice that these pins have no analog components directly under the landing pad, known as a “circuit under pad” design, making them a little less compact but more structurally resilient.

This is because these pins were originally designed to be compatible with a version of the GlobalFoundary 180nm process with only 3 metalization layers, but multiple levels of a metal structure must be present between the top metal layer where the pad is and the analog circuit beneath in order to help isolate it from the force applied to the pad of wedge bonding. During wedge bonding the bond is physically pressed in place requiring applying a lot of force to the silicon and potentially leading to breakages in the circuits underneath if sufficient structural support pillars aren’t present.

As discussed earlier, there are different families of packaging for chips resulting in different types of I/O design: flip-chips and wire bonding. Wire bonded chips such as mine have their pins facing the exterior of the chip organized in a structure called a pad ring. This is a ring surrounding the core area of the chip, connecting all the different I/O pads together. This ring is used both for noise isolation and to share power between all the different pins. Because the padring is an uninterrupted crown of pins the space between the pins is filled by very simple structures called filler cells used to close the power connections within the ring.

The IO also plays a crucial role in dealing with electrostatic discharge. (To whom many electronics have perished, including my little sister’s laptop that I may or may not have murdered while upgrading her ram when I was 15. 🪦 )

Each pin contains structures that will act as forward biased diodes in the event of an electrostatic discharge steering the charge though the power rails and protecting the sensitive core logic.

So we actually have four types of power delivery pins : two for ground and two for power.

The difference between the two groups is that one is used to provide power to the IO itself and the other is used to power the chip’s core logic.

Thus, it is possible to run the I/O and the internal design at different voltages. The areas for which a different power source is used is called a power domain. For example, the I/O could run at 5V, accepting 5V input signals and driving 5V outputs while internally the chip core runs the logic at 3.3V. In this case, we would have different pins for powering the I/O and for powering the internal core. But, in the case of this networking chip, core power is shorted to IO power and both are in the same power domains.

Such a setup is only made possible because the foundry provided 7 track standard cell library is, to put it mildly: rugged. The cell target operating range is between 1.62 and 5.5V voltage and -40 to 125C.

So shorting the IO and core voltage and deciding to run the entire thing at 5V is just an average Tuesday.

Example of a random timing report from another chip I am working on, with corners ranging from 3 to 5.5V and -40 to 125C. And again, this is still just a subset of all the corners there are: there are even more where this came from!

For reference, this is just a tiny bit unusual.

Most designs have separate power domains as modern nodes have cell libraries designed for much lower operating voltages in order to help reduce the area power density making cooling easier and to help optimize power consumption. In the case of leading edge nodes, internal logic targets operating voltages as low as 0.7 to 0.8 V. This forces having at least separate IO and core power domains, since your IO typically starts at 1.8V and above.

Yet, you sometimes need separate power domains even if they operate at the same voltage, such as cases where you want to isolate a sensitive analog block from the power supply noise caused by a quickly toggling digital part. You might even prolong this separation of an analog and digital power domains to the IO, in which case rather than having a fully connected padring working within the same power domain you would be splitting the padding into analog IO power and digital IO power.

Remember the filler cells I talked about earlier? Well there exists a special type of filler cell called a splitter used specially to split the pad ring in such cases. But, because of ESD concerns this splitter is not as simple as breaking the power line, but that is a discussion for another day.

The clock for this chip is supplied though a Schmitt trigger input pin and is strategically logged in the corner of the chip right next to the reset signal, and isolated from the rest of the pins by two power pins. This is done to limit the clock signal’s impact onto the neighboring pins given its toggle frequency, as well as to prevent the clock signal for the neighboring pins cross talk. The reset signal by comparison is a very stable signal producing little crosstalk of its own.

From this point on the clock signal is pulled into the center of the floorplan and then distributed through a balanced clock tree throughout the chip.

Such “shielding” is even more important in our case since we are doing wire bonding and we can also have cross talk between signals occurring between the fly wires, this would be less of a problem for a flip-chip package.

This is a different challenge compared to what I was doing with Tiny Tapeout as I now have access to two great resources: firstly, a lot more pins to play with, and secondly, a lot more space. Even if I target the smallest possible chip, I am still blessed with more area than I know what to do with.

Even before being invited to contribute I was already eyeing the wafer.space slots, so selecting the switch at the crown project of the ASIC was the easy choice.

The problem is that the switch was initially designed for the constraints of Tiny Tapeout. As such, not only does it have an odd architecture with only three ports, but it was designed to be as space efficient as possible. Here, space is something I am swimming in, but with only 96 hours ahead of me I have no time to redesign an entirely new switch from scratch. So the plan is to re-adapt the existing switch to make the best use of being its own chip.

The first and the most important change was to be able to make use of these abundant pins and have the switch to support more ports.

No longer shall I be constrained by my pin count! 🔥 w 🔥

… (Until I need more than 7 ports that is.)

Most of the verilog code you will see online tends to use hard coded widths like so :

What this code gains in ease of writing it loses in flexibility.

In RTL, we have a concept called parameters, which exist for an instance of a module and allow you to define, at instantiation, certain values. These values can then be used to size up buses or are macro like conditions to define which sections of the code should be included in the final hardware.

These generic values can then be inherited down the design hierarchy allowing dependent modules to be resized accordingly.

The original switch implementation was partially generic : it contained quite a few generic values, but these were mostly added out of habit to help clean up the design and keep things more readable, rather than truly making the design dimensions fully configurable.

The reason for not making the design fully generic was out of a calculated decision to shy away from as much unnecessary complexity as possible. The original design was facing the hard physical constraints of Tiny Tapeout pin count, so making it fully generic to support an arbitrary amount of ports would have been an unnecessary premature optimization, and most importantly cost complexity.

My grief against complexity comes from two calculated trade-offs.

First, I find it is orders of magnitude cheaper to add complexity than to remove it.

Secondly, complexity is especially expensive for hardware design because of the necessity to not have no have any bugs in the hardware. The only way of reaching this bug free state is through thought verification of operation under all possible scenarios. As we add complexity, we add hardware states such that the size of the space of states we need to explore grows exponentially.

Now I know exponential growth might sound like an exaggeration, after all exponential growth is so fast that it is hard for our brains to conceive, but I assure you I am not.

This problem is more formally called the “state explosion problem”.

So the biggest change in the switch was to move the number of supported ports from a static three to a generic number.

Even if the RTL scales, and I could theoretically run a simulation with 48 ports, the logic itself still has scaling limits. After all, behind the abstraction of the code we are designing hardware logic for which physical constraints still apply.

As the structures get wider, the number of logic elements on a path increases, the paths get physically longer and the timing degrades. And so, with \(1.73mm^2\) of core area available, timing is the wall I hit first.

Given the switch was already quite tight on timing, scaling it too far would push it beyond the limits of the current design requiring a rethink of the architecture. Rethink that I cannot afford to execute in so little time.

Lastly, I said I was scaling the number of ports, but because of how tight the timings are on the switch lookup table already was, it is not getting scaled up. And because it still only has four entries, and scaling beyond four ports would result in too much contention on the table and not enough hits, it would not make any sense to go beyond 4 ports for now.

Thus, I settled on four ports for the switch.

Given I now control the full ASICs layout I can also control exactly which signal maps to which pin on the padring.

Since the switch was intended to work with a specific Microchip family of external physical-layer chips, and that these chips had a known pinout, I decided to choose the pin order based on how directly I could draw the connecting wire onto the PCB.

One of the best drawbacks of the switch scaling limit was that I was left with a few pins and lots of area to play with.

And unlike with Tiny Tapeout where multiple projects share that same common infrastructure allowing only one project to be enabled at a time, this time I could have multiple designs working in parallel. And I had just the perfect project to include in parallel.

A few months back I did the two things the entire Internet knows not to do: firstly I asked Reddit for advice, secondly I followed it.

This project is called “Until Heat Death Do Us Part" and is a very serious implementation of an ethernet connected beacon that broadcasts its current time over 100 Mbit Ethernet with the ability to do so without overflow for the next \(10^{100}\) years. Also believed to be roughly the estimated heat death of the universe, give or take a few powers of 10 years.

Counting until the heat death of the universe, and broadcasting the counter every second over 100Mbps ethernet.

I have a full write-up about this ASIC’s here for those interested in getting the full story: Until Heat Death Do Us Part.

Putting it all together: this chip features two designs, the 4 port 100Mbps networking switch and the ethernet broadcast beacon. The networking switch is the denser design on the right hand side of the floorplan with the beacon being the on the left side, each designed placed next to there respective port pins.

It’s already been a few months since the chip has been sent to the fab. Since then the first batch of produced wafers have exited the fab and been received by the wafer.space.

Andrew Wingate shared with us some absolutely gorgeous pictures of the diced wafers, and there is my little chip in the flesh sitting on the top right corner of the reticle:

The dies are then picked off the diced wafer using a custom built robot and sorted per chip type into a tape reel. From there the chips will be either sent to the bond house for packaging or directly sent to the customer.

Your browser cannot play this video. Download video.

And now I am like a child waiting for Christmas, impaciently awaiting a package, inside the first batch of my own full custom ASIC chips.

Now, the chip doesn’t make a full networking equipment on its own, which is why I am also prototyping a PCB for the switch. Hopefully someday I can plug the chip in to get a fully functional switch.

Here is to hoping the first iteration of the silicon just works !

.. which anyone working in the industry can attest to, A0s are rare enough to be legendary.

Manufacturing revisions of a chip are identified by a letter followed by a number.

A0 is the first iteration, minor revision such as changing some of the higher metalization layers will increment the number and major revisions requiring a new mask set for the bottom layers, where the transistors are built, increment the letter and reset the number. So revisions might go: A0, A1, A2, B0, B1, B2, B3, C0, etc…

Meanwhile the networking equipment project continues, chasing after building increasingly complex systems. Without going too deep into which next networking features I want to add, it is becoming quickly apparent that I will need to integrate some form of a CPU.

This is because as I target more advanced networking applications the tasks my silicon needs to accomplish become increasingly varied and start featuring a large array of tasks that occur rarely enough, and have sufficiently lax performance requirements to be better suited for software than hardware.

As for the matter of which CPU architecture to choose, although RISC-V is in vogue I find that, as a result of RISC-V’s architectural choices, it is just too expensive to implement in terms of area for systems like mine.

My needs when selecting witch CPU architecture to use are:

If only gcc were to maintain something like the “Status of Supported Architectures from Maintainers’ Point of View” at https://gcc.gnu.org/backends.html then maybe I could know what my options where.

Behold: so many beautiful options supported that most people have never even heard of!

And within this list there is one 16 bit architecture that caught my eye, at the heart of one of the longest produced systems and deeply intertwined with computer history as it saw the first version of Unix written in C.

A year ago, I started on a journey to go from being solely a hardware designer to building an entire ASIC from scratch without any institutional backing.

It’s been a long road, passing though multiple smaller macro tapeouts, each allowing me to delve deeper into what it takes to make ASICs. This chip is my 10th solo tapeout, a fitting number to finally graduate into building full chips.

Standing upon this mountain I can tell you the road ahead is still very long.

And with my first batch of full custom ASICs landing into my mailbox in a few weeks a new risk has emergeded, leading me to proclaim a new goal: not starting a fabless semiconductor company.

Thanks again to wafer.space for giving me this opportunity to join the shuttle, Tiny Tapeout for making the 9 previous tapeouts possible and the open source silicon community for building the tools making all of this possible.

If you enjoyed this, I will be sipping coffee at a Silicon Valley neighborhood cafe between the 10th and 12th of November, so if you feel like nerding out over caffeine shoot me an email.

#9810. Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

Authorities seized more than 100 servers and arrested seven as part of a crackdown on a fraud network spanning more than 50 countries.

You see an online advertisement promising quick returns from trading cryptocurrency, foreign currencies, and stocks. You give the "investment firm" your information, and an operator calls you and convinces you to transfer a small amount of money into a platform. You make early profits quickly, so you deposit increasingly large sums of money. But when you attempt to withdraw your earnings, the operator stalls for a while until finally cutting off contact.

This pattern is familiar to victims of investment fraud, a multinational criminal industry that relies on social engineering to convince would-be investors that they're about to make substantial gains before pulling the rug out from under them.

Europol today shared news of the disruption of one such operation, an investment fraud scheme with potential victims across more than 50 countries and a company allegedly supplying fraudulent trading platforms and leads to criminal groups. According to a press release, Europol and Eurojust supported an international operation involving authorities in Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

The German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office led the operation, targeting a company suspected of supplying phony trading websites and multiple call centers to criminal groups; investigators estimate losses to exceed 4 million euros.

International authorities searched 17 locations, including a call center in Kosovo, leading to the seizure of 100 servers and the arrests of seven suspects.

The law enforcement action reflects a multiyear investigation that began in 2022, according to Europol, when a German couple reported they could not withdraw money invested through an online trading platform. This led to two previous "action days" by authorities, one in 2022 (involving two arrests and the seizure of evidence) and another in 2025 (involving more arrests and seizures of money and evidence).

"Analysis of the material recovered exposed the suspected infrastructure provider and its links to call centre operators, paving the way for the latest operation," the press release read.

A Eurojust press release provided further detail regarding the extent of the operation. The analysis of evidence seized during the second action day exposed a company based in Cyprus and Israel allegedly offering "crime-as-a-service," supplying criminal groups with fraudulent websites that funnel targets into the central investment scam.

The data of potential victims visiting these websites and expressing interest would be sold as leads to call centers, which contacted the victims to persuade them to invest their money, leading to repeated demands for additional investments. Authorities identified suspected call center-operating clients of this company in Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

The fraud operation guaranteed significant returns for trades in cryptocurrencies, foreign currencies, or stocks, according to Europol. But authorities found that the seemingly legitimate platforms were run by "brokers" that used phony profits and social engineering tactics to convince victims to keep investing. Additionally, investigators also found the operators used affiliate marketing services and deceptive advertisements to lure in potential victims.

Austin Anderson, director of threat intel at cybercrime disruption firm Netcraft, tells Dark Reading that operations like these that target upstream providers can help disrupt investment fraud operations at scale.

"Fraudsters have increasingly specialized in one piece of an attack's supply chain, as seen in this scheme where websites collected personal data that was sold to call centers to ultimately coerce funds from victims," he says. "While this can breed sophistication in each actor's niche, it also introduces fragility when a large dependency like the call center is disrupted. Ultimately, without arrests that remove fraudsters from the market, these operations only temporarily disrupt operations while actors rebuild their infrastructure."

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

#9809. Next-Level Benchmarking Overfitting

In my recent blog post I remarked that database benchmarking is in a crisis because AI agents start to overfit on individual benchmarks with questionable techniques, which drives execution times towards zero. This has happened with TPC-D in the past, and broke the benchmark. TPC-H tries to fight that with rules, but most people who publish (unofficial) TPC-H results simply ignore the rules. In combination with overly eager AI agents, this leads to brutal overfitting.

We are seeing the next level of that with the GenDB-V system. The corresponding paper commands “Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems”, and reports speedups of 22× to 61× over Umbra and DuckDB, and all that in a fully verified system. These are indeed impressive claims, and would suggest that traditional database engines are in trouble.

Taking a step back, though, it should be clear that a performance improvement of a factor of 22 over Umbra is infeasible, at least if we are talking about traditional query processing. At SF10, the 22 TPC-H queries read roughly 15GB of (compressed) base data, and on a 9950X3D Umbra runs all queries in a total of roughly 540ms. On that machine the memory touched for data divided by the memory bandwidth (54GB/s) alone is about 280ms; anything below that is infeasible. Better compression might bring that down a bit, but not by an order of magnitude.

Unsurprisingly, the most dramatic gains of GenDB-V come from precomputation. The agents have carefully handcrafted auxiliary data structures for each query, which are computed at load time, and which avoid most of the work. The physical design is heavily tuned to the queries, too, for example, there is an extra structure that lists the supplier rows in s_acctbal DESC order, which makes Q2 trivial. Similar per-query data structures are built for most queries. And we see that in the performance numbers: Several queries already run in near-constant time at SF100: Q2 in 0.7 ms, Q17 in about 15 ms and Q4 in about 17 ms on one thread. That is the TPC-D symptom, without stored aggregates.

There is also a “plain-array” mode, which, at first glance, is more fair, as it avoids these excessive preparations and also reports performance improvements of just roughly a factor of 3, which seems achievable. But when looking closely, we see that here the agents did something even more insane: They hard-coded their knowledge about the data generator. They “know” that each customer k will be at row k-1. And they know that dbgen numbers the i-th order 32·(i/8) + i%8, so key k should be at row 8·(k/32) + k%32 − 1. Which makes the join in query Q18 super cheap.

How does all this fit together with the claim of a fully verified database engine? Well, the code does check if the hard-coded knowledge about the data generator holds in practice, e.g., by checking if the guessed join partner row is correct. If not, it falls back to a super slow generic nested loop implementation, but as that never happens with the official TPC-H data generator, that code path is irrelevant in the reported experiments.

Which brings me back to my original blog post claim: Letting AI agents optimize for a given database benchmark makes the benchmark useless. They will do their best to find insane tricks to speed up this particular benchmark, but none of that would work in a real system. The high tuning and synthesis time aside, deleting a single tuple (or inserting one in the middle) can most likely cause the whole approach to fall off a cliff, as it forces the slow fallback path. Which is not something you want in a production system.

Stop handcrafting your engine. Start reverse-engineering dbgen!

Thank you, Thomas, for reading our paper and code so carefully. I am Jiale, one of the authors of GenDB-V. Your observations are correct, and I would like to add my view on the setting.Two settings. Umbra and DuckDB are general-purpose engines: fast for any query on any data. GenDB-V, like Bespoke OLAP and JetStream, builds a specialized engine for one customer: their schema, data, hot query templates, and even hardware. Here, using knowledge of the workload is the purpose. For ad-hoc queries, such a system should hand over to the best general-purpose engines, such as Umbra and DuckDB. So I see the two approaches as partners, not competitors. I do not claim that agents can build an engine that is fast on many workloads: just for a very specific setting, specialized for the customer. Verification is the main point. The key feature of GenDB-V is that instead of trusting agents for correctness, we can formally verify it independently. Every synthesized package is formally proved correct for every database of the schema. So each assumption must be checked in the code, and a failed check never gives a wrong answer silently: the code takes a general path. Today that path is GenDB-V's own slow proven code, but it can be easily extended to be Umbra or DuckDB.Fair and unfair specialization. I agree that guessing where dbgen puts each key is fitting to the generator, not to a customer. A property that the storage creates, or that the customer declares and the system checks, is fair. An accident of the generator is not. I will constrain the agents to the first kind.Agents also find good ideas. One example is TPC-H Q21 with agent-designed storage. The storage keeps each order's lineitems next to each other, for any input order. The EXISTS and NOT EXISTS conditions are then checked inside each order's own lineitems, in place of a semi-join and an anti-join on lineitem. No part of the query result is computed at load time. It is a classic physical-design idea that any engine could use.I fully agree that the database community needs new kinds of benchmarks, and I made one attempt in this direction in my earlier work, SQLBarber (SIGMOD 2026). I am excited to see more great benchmarks in the future. Benchmarks drove the development of today's great engines, and they can do the same in the LLM era 🙂Best,Jiale

You see I have two problems here: One is, you literally tell us to "stop handcrafting (our) engine". Which mean you are marketing your approach as a general solution and as a replacement for existing database engines, which it is clearly not. It might be an additional enhancement, like, e.g., physical design wizards did in the past. But you will always need a fallback engine, at the very least for ad-hoc queries.And second, I am pretty sure that I could build a program that computes a secure hash over the input at load time to identify that it is the canonical TPC-H data, e.g., by hard-coding all relevant scale factors, and then produces the answers to all queries purely from the knowledge about the data generator, without ever looking at the data. That would have near zero runtime for all relevant scale factors. And it would still be "correct", because I could fall back to, e.g., an embedded DuckDB/Postgres/sqlite, the performance of which would then be totally irrelevant because it would never trigger in practice.Which is clearly absurd, of course. But where do you draw the line? Why is recognizing the data set + scale factor "bad" when the other optimizations you do are not? TPC-H tries to codify this, which works to varying degrees _if_ people follow the rules (which many don't). I think we can only fight this if a) the benchmark is unknown to the engine developer before execution, and b) the data changes over time, which rules out the most extreme precomputations.

If formal verification is the main contribution, why are the headline results dominated by 20–60× speedups? Verification establishes correctness, but what does it tell us about the validity of those performance comparisons?

It is an honour to discuss this with you here. As a PhD student, I admire your work, and Umbra is one of my favourite systems and papers. I am sorry for the title: it describes a possible future as if it were a present fact. I will discuss changing it with my co-authors.GenDB-V has two modes. Template synthesis builds specialized code for hot templates. That mode is an addition to a general-purpose engine, as physical design wizards were. Engine synthesis builds one general engine, proved correct for any schema, data and query in the supported SQL subset. In coverage and correctness it is a complete query engine for that subset. In performance it is not there yet: agents improved it over many versions, first on TPC-H and then on a second benchmark, but on manually created unseen queries it is still slower than Umbra. I will put its code and results in our repository.My next step is an adversarial loop. Agents optimize the engine on all the benchmarks I have. Then the engine is frozen, and a separate adversarial agent writes new workloads against it: new queries on the known benchmarks, and completely new benchmarks. I report the frozen engine's result. After that, the agents may optimize on the queries where it lost, and the next round brings a new attack. The open question is whether the gap on unseen workloads shrinks over the rounds, that is, whether agents can build an engine that truly generalizes. This is in the spirit of your proposal of fresh workloads for each round.On the line: your example is a good test. The proof checker ensures correctness for every possible database, and nothing more. Your program would not pass it. A hash has a fixed size, so different databases can share a hash value; a secure hash is good enough in practice, but a mathematical proof must hold for all databases. Falling back to a production SQL engine cannot pass either, because none comes with proofs today; so currently GenDB-V falls back to its own engine, which is verified but slow. But I agree that the proof says nothing about performance: an optimization is correct for every database, and fast only for some. So the proof does not draw the whole line. Your (a) fits general-purpose engines; in the specialized setting the hot templates are known by design. Your (b) applies to both: a customer's data also changes, so the speed should hold on data the agent has never seen.What I want to suggest is a direction: agents write code and proofs together, checked against a formal specification of SQL. Our proofs are only as good as our SQLSpec, which is our own reading of SQL. So I would like to invite the community to work on a shared, standard formal semantics for SQL. With it, verified engines and verified optimizations become possible for everyone, and maybe one day agents can bring a verified engine close to hand-built ones.

I don't think "correct SQLSpec" can solve the hardcoding dbgen logic problem Thomas pointed out. At the end of the day, you are verifying a database "correct", which has nothing to do with performance. In production, performance is part of correctness -- if a distribution drift of customer data causes a critical query to become orders of magnitude slower (as the example case would), that is a bug and an outage. The most egregious thing I find about this work is the attempt to portray formal verification as a green checkmark next to an arbitrary system, and disregard the fact that it proves a much narrower mathematical property that is highly sensitive to the exact formal definitions and assumptions with many pitfalls. P.S. I generally like to assume the best of intentions from researchers, but I find your replies to sound a lot like AI.

Hi, I never claim that formal verification can ensure performance, both in the paper and in my previous responses. The ONLY thing formal verification can ensure is that, the results returned by the code, is allowed by the outcome specified in SQLSpec, and that is all.For performance, we can only rely on benchmark feedback to guide the optimization, and as the final metric, not formal verification. Then we have the issue with benhmark evaluation: agents or systems overfitting to the benchmark, though in some cases, we want such specialization for customized code for hot templates.PS: I give you my word, all the intentions from my previous comments come from me. I did use AI to re-write my draft, and the prompt is "make it simple, clear, and concise", and by Fable 5.2, and that is all. If we do not like the "AI-Style", from now on, I will use my original draft. Or if you want more, you can have a meeting with me to discuss more

You didn't even understand why the previous one said that "performance" should be part of "correctness".

All the optimizations for the hot paths, are checked at runtime: (1) If the data changes and the assumption does not hold anymore, the specialized code will never be executed. (2) If the fallback system is a powerful general-purpose engine, such as Umbra or DuckDB, this query would not be orders of magnitude slower.

Given all your clarifications, why is synthesizing a standalone database engine the right abstraction in the first place?If the goal is hot-query specialization, existing engines already offer workload-aware physical design, materialization, query compilation, and other optimization techniques. Coding agents can also help engineers implement and test new optimizations within these engines.What concrete capability does GenDB-V provide that cannot be achieved more economically by augmenting an existing engine? And what evidence demonstrates that advantage?

"All the optimizations for the hot paths, are checked at runtime: (1) If the data changes and the assumption does not hold anymore, the specialized code will never be executed. (2) If the fallback system is a powerful general-purpose engine, such as Umbra or DuckDB, this query would not be orders of magnitude slower."------Well I guess the point is. If your agent is overfitting too much, then the solution will be very sensitive to specific benchmark features. This means that, if the workload got drifted, even by a little bit, your solution will fail the checker and you can only fall back. Ofc you can use a faster backend engine, but if your agent is falling-back in 99.9% of the time (ofc in more realistic, drifted workloads, not a fixed one), where is your contribution? I feel one major point of previous discussions is that, you don't have systematic and reasonable enough evaluation, and people doubt you over-claiming.

“This means that, if the workload got drifted, even by a little bit, your solution will fail the checker and you can only fall back.”------Well, he can always add another "smart" agent to handle workload drift.

For hot-query specialization by coding agents, it is not a new claim from GenDB-V (but from previous GenDB, Bespoke OLAP, and JetStream), so I will not discuss more on this. I like the discussions in Bespoke OLAP paper: there are some advantages from directly implementing specialized code compared to tuning an existing system.For the abstraction of synthesizing a standalone database engine, isn't this itself an interesting and exciting direction to explore, as a research project? One important "economical benefit" of GenDB-V, I would say formal verification. No production SQL engine is formally verified to the best of my knowledge (correct me if I am wrong). It was so difficult and expensive to formally verify something: seL4’s 8,700-line C kernel took about 20 person-years! And now it is possible, to have a formally verified standalone database engine, and we achieve this in a much cheaper way, isn't this exciting?BTW, just to give some contexts in case some people are not familiar with formal verification: formal verification does not mean "bug-free", just the code is verified against the formal specification, which is SQLSpec in GenDB-V. I do not claim this spec is correct. So I open-source it and hope the community could fix and refine it together.

"I feel one major point of previous discussions is that, you don't have systematic and reasonable enough evaluation, and people doubt you over-claiming."------I totally agree that I over-claimed for performance. The honest performance claim should be that, the synthesized engine can outperform untuned general-purpose engine, on a specific target .I will update the claims. And I will run new experiments, with more strict settings and evaluations. Happy to take any suggestions. For example, the tool from Microsoft to generate skewed TPC-H data, and this is totally invisible to agents during synthesis?BTW, I am always open to feedbacks, discussions, and suggestions, and will always improve based on these. Just hope, the discussion is open, healthy, friendly, and not emotional 🙂

#9808. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

Visual document retrieval and RAG with NeoMME-Retriever

Visual document retrieval and RAG with NeoMME-Retriever

#9807. Barracuda’s email security gateways bitten by make-me-root vulns

Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges.

“We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory.

Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.”

The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week.

CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface.

As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.”

CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG).

“If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either.

We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems.

These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities.

#9806. A faster Easter date function

This post is a fun little side quest to kickstart my journey optimising regional calendars.

Computing the date of Easter faster is not going to matter in any real application. Even in places where it might seem to matter, like high frequency trading applications, it is probably better to just use an in-memory lookup table for holiday dates...However, no "Fast Date" series would be complete without some mention of this classic problem.

The rules for Easter were broadly decided at the First Council of Nicaea, organised by Emperor Constantine in 325 AD, ultimately landing on the first Sunday after the first full moon, on or after March 21. Later, for operational efficiency, the church defined "full moon" according to a formula, which was eventually modified by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 ("Gregorian Easter"), with the first Easter under the new rules applying in most Catholic countries the following year.The Church of England first observed the new date of Easter in 1753, but Eastern / Orthodox churches continue to follow the old rules.

This article is about the new "Gregorian" Easter, because it is much more complex and slow to compute. For more details on the underlying algorithm, you can see Gauss's Algorithm on Wikipedia (the first known self-contained function, which basically all later algorithms build on).

The code below runs really fast.It's around twice as fast as a standard easter function that you might find in a typical date library, and I suspect it may be the fastest one made so far ð¤·.Part of that speed is attributable to using only 5 multiplications (whereas typical reference algorithms have 10 or more multiplications).

The accuracy range of around -11m â +16m years might seem a bit of overkill, but the reason I targeted this range is so that any date library that expresses dates via a signed or unsigned 32âbit "rata die", is covered by this function. This means that if you decide to not clamp the logic to years after 1582, at least it will return something resembling the correct rules, rather than garbage.

Note that this function contains more terms than traditional Easter functions, but bear in mind that the compiled assembly will be a lot smaller. So if you don't care about the speed, but want a tiny impact on binary size, that could be a reason to consider this function.

The rest of this post will briefly explain the tricks used in this function:

You'll notice that the very first thing we do is add a strange value SHIFT to the input value. This is done for two reasons:

For example, most Easter algorithms have a term like (5 + 8 * c) / 25, where c is the century (year / 100 + 1). The term 25 in the calculation of shift is responsible for aligning the century such that the constant 5 can be removed, resulting in c * 8 / 25, which is then approximated in the final algorithm with a single mul-shift: (u64) c * M25 >> 32.

Other terms in SHIFT: 19, 400, 30 are all doing similar things related to the 19-year-cycle, 400-year-cycle, and mod-30 steps.The term * 2 is different. Without this term, the range of coverage would be -5,403,600 â +22,363,835; which doesn't quite cover the range we wanted, which for signed 32-bit rata die, is Â±5.88m years. Including * 2 increases the value of shift by exactly 5,700,000, which is how many years it takes for the Easter pattern to repeat, and gets the range we are after.

If you like this type of optimisation, but are not a fan of the low-level bit-shifting and so on, then you might prefer to use this function here below. It is a much more readable version of the function, which only has these higher-level optimisations applied.

Note that unlike in the main function presented earlier, MOD 30 needs to be a positive-modulus function (even for positive dates), and that the nextSunday helper is anchored to the internal logic of the function, not related to Unix day-counting.

Note: a variant in the C++ repo has some small optimisations not shown here (fast day-of-week and fast mod 30), and a range of [-73,803,600 .. 70,208,581].

Computing year % 19 is a staple of Easter algorithms.It's related to the Metonic cycle, where every 19 years there are nearly exactly 235 full moons.

It is traditionally used in Easter algorithms in two ways:

We are going to compute these same things using a single multiplication.These steps seem unavoidable at first, but they can be eliminated. We'll begin by expanding the first one:

(11 * (year % 19) + ... ) MOD 30(11 * (year - year / 19 * 19) + ... ) MOD 30(11 * year - year / 19 * 209 + ... ) MOD 30(11 * year + year / 19 + ... ) MOD 30

The last step there might be the least obvious. It works because we can add any multiple of 30 to the multiplier and get the same result (a property of MOD), so add 30 Ã 7 = 210, which means we can remove the multiplication by 209 and just invert the sign.

This leaves us with only two terms related to year which can be computed efficiently in parallel, however using a 64âbit multiplier, we can actually merge these into one (fixed-point multiplication by 11 1/19):

u64 constexpr M19 = (1 << 32) / 19 + 1 + (11 << 32)((year * M19 >> 32) + ... ) MOD 30

This is the only 64âbit multiplication in the function, and a 32-bit compiler should have no trouble turning that back into the previous pair of multiplications.

The algebra above relies on MOD 30, which is different to % 30 in C for negative numbers.The value being computed does not go negative over our range, so the substitutions remain valid.

Now on to the other term: (year % 19) > 10. It is a well known trick to use the low bits from the mul-shift of division by 19 as a comparison cutoff, and the version used in my function is u32(b) > 0x90000000. The extra term in our multiplier (11 << 32) has no effect in the lower 32âbits, so this still works. Cassio Neri has written about things like this, if you want to read more you can start with this Overload Edition 154 .

So, this is just one multiplication plus the MOD 30, which is usually an additional two multiplications, but we'll eliminate those later in Trick #4.

There's always a % 7 term in these Easter functions, which is then subtracted from a final result. This is because Easter is on the âfirst Sunday after [...]â.

Clearly we are going to use the fast-mod-7 trick from the weekday article. If you haven't read that article, you should. You won't understand this section otherwise, and frankly, it's a better article than this one.

The same mod-7 trick as before, but notice that the mapping is reversed? (The numbers track anti-clockwise)

So why not just subtract the result of % 7 like everybody else? Well, that would make the final line be: j - m + C (for some constant C). This does not fit the pattern of a single-operation LEA instruction on x86.

Instead, we adapt the fast-mod-7 code to use a fixed-point multiplier of 6 / 7 (rather than 1 / 7) before the right-shift-29, which means this line actually counts mod-7 backwards for us! This means the final line can be j + m + C, which fits LEA and saves... one cycle ð (depending on the compiler and CPU...).

This one is pretty obvious if you've been following this blog series.MOD 30 can be calculated faster by using our favourite identity:

This was introduced and proven in the weekday article, and utilised more notably in the time-of-day article.Here setting D = 30, c = 2 gives us the useful version where we can apply MOD 32 (same as & 31).

This final bit, I'm not sure if it's been done before exactly like this.

Easter can only ever be in March or April (month 3 or 4), and luckily March is 31 days long, which means we can use % 32 to truncate dates there. A straightforward modulus would cause March 32 to overflow to April 0, a non-existent date, so we add the term v >> 7 which increments the date when it overflows (a lucky coincidence relying on April, month 4, being a power-of-2).

I have seen similar things done before using % 31, but I have not seen this with the clean bit-mask approach.

So, that's it. A bunch of fussing about to make a simple streamlined function that is next to impossible to read... but fast.

This article was prompted by Twitter/X user Dirk Loss replying to one of my posts with a link to a ChatGPT thread, where he used AI to compute Easter faster. See ChatGPT thread.

The AI actually did a pretty good job. It used learnings from my prior blog posts to apply various optimisations, but also came up with new twists on these ideas. It produced a function that is really fast, and that is accurate over the range 1498â14,544. The range is a fairly reasonable choice given that the modern rules for Easter took effect after 1582, and nobody really needs Easter further into the future.

In a serious case of "Not Invented Here" syndrome (on behalf of human kind), I had to see if I could beat the AI. I clearly did, otherwise there wouldn't be this blog post. The wider-range algorithm presented in this article has around 5-15% higher throughput across tested platforms, and similar latency (despite the wider range).

My algorithm was adapted from the one presented in Calendrical Calculations (Reingold and Dershowitz).I did not apply any learnings from the ChatGPT one, though we settled on several similar steps.

I suspect this function could be optimised more, as it still has the same overarching structure of existing algorithms going back a very long time.I tried for a little while to find a shortcut solution using the Python "Z3 Theorem Prover", which found an alternative which is a further 15-20% faster than my main one, however it's only accurate over a micro range [1894 .. 2199]. It is available in the testcase repo . If you can find a function of similar or faster speed with a wider range, feel free to let me know and I will update the repo and this page!

Although I beat the AI in this case, itâs a pretty mild victory as it was just a basic model with a moderate amount of compute. Itâs sad to know that if frontier models were pointed at the problems Iâve been tackling in this blog series, they would probably unearth every last jewel of optimisation left in the blink of an eye. I hope that I have time to explore this space more before it becomes barren.

If you enjoyed this post, you should follow me on X to get notified when I publish more date and algorithm related articles.

Exhaustive tests of the ranges asserted in this article can be verified via the testcase code: https://github.com/benjoffe/fast-world-calendars .

The same repository is used for benchmarking, where a large set of random years are loaded into memory and tested.

All results were obtained by running the benchmark with -repeat=10 and recording the median results.The -batch flag runs each computation 3 times before loading the next entry from memory. This ensures that the processor is not bottlenecked by memory access.Latency results use the same command but replace the batch flag with -latency. This mode feeds the result of each computation into the next, so there is no parallelisation.

The number in a small font size represents the number of nanoseconds per year computation.The larger number is the ratio of these results compared to the New function as a baseline.

Note: the benchmarks compute "Days since 22 March" (not day and month), as some of the reference algorithms only return this value.If my optimisation of the day/month step is novel, then the speedup would be larger than presented here.

InfoQ Homepage News Google Cloud Spend Caps Reach General Availability with API and Monthly Resets

Nov 10, 2026 3 min read

Google Cloud has made spend caps generally available on Cloud Billing Budgets, letting customers pause new usage of a service in a project once a monthly budget is reached, without deleting resources. The GA release adds an API, estimated live costs that trigger caps within minutes for AI services, and automatic monthly resets, but enforcement remains limited to Gemini API, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions.

A spend cap is a budget with enforcement attached: according to the documentation, when estimated spend on the capped service reaches the target amount, new requests to that service in that project are blocked, in-flight requests run to completion and are charged, persistent resources keep running, and nothing is deleted. Usage covered by committed-use discounts is paused along with pay-as-you-go usage, while Provisioned Throughput for AI models is never halted. Billing administrators and project owners receive alerts at 50, 80, and 100 percent of the cap.

The company changed three things between the July public preview and the GA release:

The limits are as specific as the features: a cap covers one project and one service for a calendar month, so folders, organizations, labels and multi-service budgets are out of scope, as are reseller accounts and subscription charges such as Gemini Enterprise seats. The estimate that drives enforcement is calculated at list price and excludes credits and discounts. Enforcement is also not instant: the documentation states that "any cost overages are billed as normal" and advises setting the cap "slightly below your absolute limit." Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, and networking are not among the eligible services, which means the cap addresses a runaway model or agent loop and not a forgotten GPU instance.

The narrower scope drew criticism when the preview expanded in October. On a Hacker News thread, one commenter who had asked Google for the capability a year earlier to control AI spend called the result "very crude, not granular like the rich IAM system," noting the four-product, month-only design. Another observed that Cloud Run had been added that morning, so the service list was still growing.

Developer Simon Willison argued in October that pay-by-usage services should default to hard caps, because coding and personal agents make it far easier to spin up code that calls paid APIs, and that "most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill." He cited Google's caps alongside a project-level spend limit in AWS's new account experience, which pauses the whole project and stops its resources when reached, preserving data for 90 days, and which AWS is rolling out to a limited number of customers. Azure's spending limit remains confined to free accounts and credit-based subscriptions; Microsoft states it isn't available for subscriptions with commitment plans or with pay-as-you-go pricing.

Spend caps pair with early anomalies, a daily baseline model that flags directional cost variances per service and names the top SKUs behind a spike, which Google positions as the detection half of the same control loop. Both are configured from the Budgets and Alerts page in the Billing console or through the Budgets API.
