#9783. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9782. Seven stable kernels with fixes for three Xen vulnerabilities

Hot on the heels of the previous two stable kernels, Greg Kroah-Hartman has announced the release of the 7.3.3, 6.18.62, 6.12.116, 6.6.162, 6.1.192, 5.15.225, and 5.10.274 stable kernels. Each one only contains fixes for three use-after-free vulnerabilities announced today by the Xen security team.

Two of the vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to cause a denial of service (DoS) for the entire Xen host machine with possible information leakage (CVE-2026-100080, CVE-2026-100082), and one may allow privilege escalation as well as a DoS of the host machine (CVE-2026-100081). Users should, of course, upgrade if they are using Xen.

Note: you can avoid this step in the future by logging into your LWN account.

#9781. What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

In this video conversation, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from an ill-conceived phishing simulation to a hacktivist attack on a US government agency.

Phishing tests can be an important part of cybersecurity awareness training. But as the NBA champion New York Knicks recently showed, they can also go awry.

According to a recent report in The Athletic, Madison Square Garden (MSG) Sports, which owns the Knicks, deployed a poorly timed and ill-conceived phishing simulation ahead of its banner-raising ceremony on Oct. 20. MSG Sports sent out emails to employees with offers of free championship rings commemorating the team's historic NBA Finals victory in June.

Team employees often receive championship rings at the start of the following season. However, the emails in this case were part of a phishing simulation, and when employees clicked on the links to select their rings, they were informed they failed the test and had to attend mandatory cybersecurity training. And they didn't get the rings, either.

Dark Reading senior writer Alex Culafi and senior news director Rob Wright discuss the situation on this episode. Also on tap: a hacktivist group breached the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and published personnel records for more than 40,000 employees, and it's unclear how the agency was compromised; and a New York Times report claims a NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles; and, sign up for the Dark Reading newsletter!

#9780. Weird licenses and the new open source

Somewhere on an IRC channel, I ended up in a conversation about the The Filthy Human Hands (FHH) License. It wasn't the first time weird licenses were discussed there: Reticulum's sparked some interesting discussions as well.

If you don't want to read the Wikipedia article on Free Software, a couple of years ago, I gave a small presentation at school as part of the "Oral communication in English" course, which is a (shoddy) cake-based explanation of the topic. Long story short, a Free Software is a software with 4 freedoms:

There is also the term Open Source, which is more or less Free Software but without the sociopolitical aspect of it, which is like a pizza without olives, or art without context: something devoid of meaning, a business-oriented product instead of a creation. Like in every sociopolitical endeavour, people sometimes disagree, leading to subtle but important variations. One of the most important one in the Free Software movement has been the question of the copyleft: should derivatives of Free Software be licensed under the same license? Some licenses, like the GPL says yes and this includes everything built on top of GPL code, the LGPL says that only code under LGPL needs to be released as LGPL, and others, called permissive licenses, like the BSD and MIT don't impose such restrictions.

The Free Software movement started in 1986, so we're around 40 years later now, and the picture is pretty bleak: technically, one could argue that it won, as every computer-using company in the world depends on Free Software one way or the other: Firefox, Linux, VLC, Chrome, Ubuntu, Apache, nginx, Wikipedia, Open Street Map, Open Food Facts, â¦ as well as more fundamental software components like curl, libxml, busybox, OpenSSL, GCC, clang, â¦

Yet virtually none of them do contribute back to those commons, some of them being thanklessly maintained by a random person in Nebraska. Worse, a handful of computer-related companies ("cloud providers") are making ungodly amount of money renting infrastructure running Free Software, most smartâ¢ devices are running Free Software, every single software producing/selling company depends on Free Software, and again, almost none contribute back meaningfully. A small number are trying to sponsor some projects they're depending on, but it often feels like a crass move for software that are maintained as a hobby: "Could you please garden a bit more efficiently, and add 150 apple trees to your small garden? We need it for our business, here is a 1000â¬ one-time payment"

With AI making everything worse, Free Software maintainers are now wasting their time dealing with unreviewable useless pull-requests, drowning into a sea of low-quality no-fix-provided bug reports, being demoralized by vibe-coded forks adding shiny features that are never going to be upstreamable and thus upstreamed. It really feels as if nobody is even contemplating making the pedestrian effort of trying to avoid murdering the golden goose.

Copyleft does help to mitigate those behaviours a bit, as companies aren't usually big fans to having to release their secret source code. The Asahi Linux project recently re-licensed its software from MIT to LGPL, to make it, if only symbolically, harder for people to profit from the labor without giving anything back. Unfortunately, there are a handful of tricks to bypass copyleft: don't use GPL as all, use strong boundaries (like Android is doing: Linux for its kernel, but everything running on top of it can have whatever license), rent the software to the users (every Cloud is doing that, and most ISP too), provide a context-free dump of the modifications and prevent users from modifying the code their devices are running, simplify ignore the license as the odds of somebody suing you are low, â¦

If copyleft isn't the answer, maybe it's time to find better licenses? In my opinion, the freedom 0, being able to run the program for whatever purpose, might be the crux of the problem. Reticulum's license has the following paragraph, because of course a decentralised secure communication network could help killing people more efficiently:

The Software shall not be used in any kind of system which includes amongst its functions the ability to purposefully do harm to human beings.

This sounds reasonable in theory, but it means that it's not Free anymore. Do we care? Well, Linux distributions usually have strict policies (debian, fedora, â¦) when it comes to what software they package, with non-Free ones being either forbidden, on living in their own not-enabled-by-default dedicated repository.

One step further is the The Filthy Human Hands (FHH) License, with:

No part of a work under this license may be used or reproduced in any manner by organizations or businesses with more than fifty (50) employees. An exception is granted to allow ISPs and other hosting services to reproduce the work for the purposes of display and distribution.

No part of a work under this license may be used or reproduced in any manner which promotes bigotry of any kind. This includes but is not limited to fascism, racism, sexism, misogyny, ableism, transphobia (including erasure and/or denial of nonbinary identities), homophobia, ageism, sane-ism (including denial of multiplicity and/or plurality), and discrimination against non-human identities.

What's interesting here, from a technical point of view, is that this isn't really enforceable, legally speaking, as most terms are pretty vague. I think it's by design, and must be taken as a statement. One could use any other open-to-interpretation terms and obtain the same effects, namely that any entity with a legal department won't use it, and those small enough to not have one won't be able to sell/rent to those who do. What's beautiful about it, is that it does fit perfectly into the idea of the small web, of small communities with bespoke governance, of bricolage and of excluding authoritarianism/capitalism/morons/â¦ by design.

Given the current dire state of the world, I think it's time to realise that Free Software isn't enough, and that not wanting to have code ending up in whatever war machine bombing kids and families is less radical than the idea of Free Software at its inception 40 years ago. I'd love a weird-license repositories in Linux distributions with lovely, quirky, useful, useless, handcrafted software!

#9779. [$] Locking down hibernation for the winter

When a computer hibernates, the kernel writes the contents of memory to disk and then shuts the system down. Resuming from hibernation involves reading that data back into memory, and then having the kernel pick up where it left off. Unfortunately, the kernel does not have any way to know that the data it is reading back has not been tampered with, which is why lockdown, an optional kernel feature that attempts to prevent modifications to the running kernel, disables hibernation. Matthew Garrett, who has been working on lockdown for many years, has shared a patch set that aims to fix this problem. His solution must also protect against downgrade attacks (where an attacker reboots the computer with an older kernel version to bypass new protections), which complicates the implementation.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Batch Intelligence at Scale: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience

Aditya Mulik explains how Walmart Global Tech deployed multi-agent LLM workflows across 4,700 stores for nightly batch inventory forecasting. He discusses tackling production hurdles - schema violations, cross-department data mismatches, and network drops - via MCP grounding and loop agents, while slashing cloud inference costs from $100k+ to $10k per month shifting from PTUs to pay-as-you-go.

Aditya Mulik is a Senior Software Engineer at Walmart Global Tech specializing in large-scale distributed systems and platform engineering, with deep expertise in deploying scalable and resilient solutions. He has led the development of microservices architectures and production LLM systems, enabling high-throughput applications serving millions of requests. He also contributes to open source.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Aditya Mulik: My topic today is, Batch Intelligence at Scale, which is, Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience. My name is Aditya Mulik. I work as a senior software engineer at Walmart Global Tech.

The problem I want to walk you through today is one which all retailers are wrestling with right now, which is inventory accuracy. What I want to say is the retail at massive scale, so Walmart has around 4,700 stores within the U.S. They have multiple stores in Canada, Mexico, and so on as well, but the major chunk is in the U.S. itself. There are hundreds of thousands of SKUs. There are varying departments, like varying products, any product that we can imagine of, those are all available at Walmart. The physical space is also quite large and so many items have to be tracked very carefully. The problem that each retailer is dealing with, as I mentioned about inventory accuracy, is where we have to determine what is the right inventory required for a particular occasion. If it's Thanksgiving, we have to make sure that much inventory is available at a particular point in time.

What I want to mention over here is, can we predict what inventory a department needs? I'm particularly looking for a particular department here. Can we predict what inventory a department needs for the next n number of days accurately, automatically, and at scale? Because the scale is quite large, and if you are targeting a particular department, it has to have a particular set of items available. If you are walking towards a shelf and if that shelf doesn't have a particular item available, it's not a good experience. We have to ensure that each item has to be available and in stock.

The accuracy imperative. Accuracy isn't a nice-to-have, it's very mission critical, on any particular item. What we worked on was fresh food, or basically the items, you can take an example like rotisserie chicken or fresh beef, these items can expire very quickly. The store manager has to decide very accurately like, what items are there in stock and what items need to be ordered, to make sure that the inventory is very accurate for the next n number of days. The line between a stock shelf and an empty rack is what we are looking over here right now. If there are stockouts or overstock, then it could be a problem. If it's an overstock, obviously the items are going to go to waste. Either it has to be donated or it has to be thrown away. Consider this compounded across millions of square feet of retail. We have 4,700 stores, so you can imagine how critical this could be for a particular store. The next thing I'll say here is, how do we keep inventory accurate at this scale? Our first answer has to be an obvious one, we have to forecast the demand based on the history.

Now the thing is like, in Walmart, we already have machine learning models which can actually predict the amount of inventory that has to be ordered. We have backward-looking machine learning models which are trained on historical sales data to forecast future demand. We use like a year's or maybe two years of sales data, where we are trying to determine, ok, this much amount of inventory has to be ordered for the next maybe 30 days or maybe next 60 days, and so on. It's reliable for steady, recurring, and seasonal trends. Walmart is very focused on Thanksgiving. We know during Thanksgiving we have to order n number of items. That is very accurate for prediction. It's fully automated and it scales across SKUs and stores. The problem right now is sales forecasting accuracy. The pro over here is like, based on the historical trends, it can get it properly.

What if there are blind unprecedented events. Consider an example where there's a storm coming. Now the machine learning model won't be able to accurately determine if there's a storm, and if we need water or certain other items. Will that be actually available well in advance? That machine learning model might not be able to predict that. These are the things that the store manager has to deal with. They can't just rely on this particular backward trend. The question became, how do we add real-time, real-world context on top of the signals we already trust. The thing is, since we already have the machine learning models and we already know the prediction can be done in a specific way, this was an engineering challenge that came on to us, where we had to determine how should we just not rely on backward trends. Like, this is something that's going to happen, and then this number of stock has to be ordered. What if we can add some real-time context to it?

That's where we came up with a multi-agent — not monolith — basically a sequential workflow of agents where this agentic flow can actually determine, like get the real-time data along with some forecasting model data as well, and get the exact accurate decision that has to be given to the store manager, where these are the number of items that they need to order. How did we do that? Basically, in the sequential agentic workflow, we added multi-agent orchestration, like one agent after another, where first agent would determine, so in this case, it gathers context from various data sources for a particular department. Consider if it's a department, or like as I said about the fresh food, it's getting all the metadata from various sources like BigQuery and so on. That context is then fed to the agent, which outputs more accurate data. If it's like rotisserie chicken, it has to be ordered for the quantity that needs to be determined.

Then the second agent consumes that data, and then it synthesizes past sales data prepared by the data engineering pipeline. We have another pipeline which is set to get more context. What it does is, there's an amalgamation of two datasets which is collated, and then it is fed to another third agent data. Now this agent is quite important, which analyzes the context and output from the previous agent, and there is a grounding mechanism over here now. Consider, as I said, just a backward ML trend is not going to get us the exact prediction. There might be a weather agent, or there might be some weather API call. There could be a trending event that's happening, a sales event is happening over there. It can gather that context and it can make more accurate predictions, now that it has to order more or either less of the inventory. Then, finally, the fourth agent which produces the final natural language recommendation directive, which is like, increase the stock by this percent, and so on. That's the entire sequential workflow that we created. This was particularly targeted for a specific department.

Going to the next part, so the output, and this is the human-in-the-loop. What we were trying to do over here was, all this context generation and everything was fine, but our only goal was the store manager has to get a clear directive. The clear directive was not a dashboard, it was just a clear command. Increase apple stock 15% in produce ahead of the weekend. They are having a clear context on what they need to do. It's not just that, they are just going to increase the stock right away. There's a real-time data integration as I mentioned, which is like, MCP lets agents pull live data sources during reasoning. All of that is verified using live tools, MCPs, and so on, which is grounded properly. The critical checkpoint is, the store manager reviews each recommendation, and the store manager can either accept it or override it, because they will manually go and check and verify if there is actually a shortage of apples, if they do want to order it. There was a human in the loop in this entire pattern. This is a feature not a fallback. Human oversight in the final validation layer was catching the local context that the data cannot. That was the additional validation that the store manager was doing.

Now this is where the important aspect comes. Then we went to production. The pilot was magic, because we tested it on maybe 10 stores or 15 stores, and then we had a clear output, coherent recommendations, and the stakeholders were quite happy about it. Then we flipped the switch to full-scale nightly runs. This was not like a real-time context where the store manager is communicating with the app, it's just a recommendation that the store manager gets during the start of the day. As Walmart stores open in the early morning, they get this recommendation and then they act upon it. Yes, we did this. We went to full chain, like all 4,700-plus stores that we rolled it out to. Then, what works at the scale of one rarely survives the scale of thousands. Here are the four failures that taught us why. Because we saw that, ok, we went to production, we made it like full chain available.

Initially for a 10-store pilot, recommendations were great, we got good feedback. There were a lot of engineering teams, data science team getting involved, and they had everything analyzed. The main thing was, me and my team's task was to get it to production, and then we started observing a lot of failures. There were four main failures which taught us what exactly happened.

I'm moving on towards the failures now. These are the common failures that we have always seen in the LLM world, and this is how we also tackled it. The very first one was hallucinations and schema violations. Here as you can see, hallucinations and schema violations were like, we had to enforce structured outputs, because the agentic workflow was getting the context, it was getting all the data, the output as well. The output was vague at times, because it was not always validated how it has to be given to the end user. Here you can see like we had to add some schema layer, which is basically to validate outputs via some JSON format of identical validation. I can give a bad example output over here. This was one of the recommendations that went to one of the store managers. As you can see over here, I think you should probably increase some stock for the weekend, maybe around 15% or so, for produce items that sell well.

We don't know. It's just saying that around 15%, and it should be about something that's in the produce section. Now the store manager has to go and verify which is the item that's low on stock. This didn't make sense, and it still gave a pretty high confidence. The thing is it did validate across the schema but it didn't make sense from a good output perspective. What we did is we fixed it with structured output, but also making sure that the item is also validated across a specific SKU, whether it's like which department it belongs to. If it's a produce, the item name has to be there, which is the Honeycrisp Apple right over there, and the SKU.

This confidence level made sure like this is adhering to the department that it has to be. This can be extended as possible. The stock directive, the schema which is given, and this is all validated across a common schema. As I mentioned, here's the same output. Now schema enforced, every field typed and validated: the exact SKU, item, department, and adjustment. No ambiguity left. This was the first failure.

Then, again, now the second failure. This is something that we encountered once we were full chain as well, where it was semantically wrong. What do we mean by that? You're ensuring data integrity with semantic validation. Even though we did have structured output there was a problem. The problem was the data engineering, because the workflow that was created was an overnight job, where we gathered data from various sources. Walmart has so much data for each produce, or each department. Once we pull the data, there were certain things that were getting mapped properly but certain things were not getting mapped accurately. This was a one-off situation maybe out of hundreds of items that we found out there was an issue. I can give an example over here. As you see here, everything is matching to the schema, but as we can see I have highlighted over here.

At Walmart there are multiple departments. The SKUs are unique as well, but the problem is it can map one of the items which has the same item number, but the department is different. The other department might have the same item number. The only varying part is the department over here. If there's a product that's coming as Honeycrisp Apple, but it is coming from auto_parts, so there should be some recommendation for auto_parts which was showing to the end user, but for an auto_part it was showing as a Honeycrisp Apple, which doesn't make sense. This was a failure at the data ingestion layer, where basically, wherever the data was being fetched from, it was not correctly being mapped. We had to also validate if the SKU is correct and also the item name is also coming from the same SKU. This was one of the failures. It was a dangerous kind of failure, perfectly valid JSON, but it maps Honeycrisp Apple to auto_parts because the SKUs collided.

The schema can't catch this, only schema validation can. How did we ensure to fix this? This is the part where we did the grounding mechanism. As you can see, we introduced an MCP tool call over here, basically validate coherence, where if you are getting a stock directive, we have an MCP client which is connecting to the proper data source. From that proper data source, we are looking up the proper catalog that belongs to that item. We made sure that any item that is not relevant to that particular data pipeline, it should not be processed as well. That's where we ensured, ok, this is something that every output coming from an agent has to be validated with some grounding mechanism. This was another failure that we encountered.

Then there was one more. This is the place where it's very common, where outputs were vanished. What do I mean by that? Over here you can see unreliable inference, which is failure disrupts perfect inferences, and then there is resilient inference. What I mean by that is there could be network issues, like network partition can happen as we know. Here you can see we had some logs enabled. Because in the pipeline, the way it was, there are multiple agents doing multiple tasks, and then their task was to just save the output to some persistent storage. What if there is a db_write failure, like here you can see clearly there is a timeout error which is the connection reset that has happened. Because of the connection reset the output has just vanished now. We didn't have a mechanism initially where if the output is vanished, maybe there are like 4700 stores, maybe some of the stores were not even saving the output and the store manager was just opening the app, and seeing like, ok, there's no recommendation today, that means everything is proper.

That was a failure that was observed. How did we fix that as well? This is where the mechanism of the agentic workflow agent comes over here. We had a sequential agent, and we then determined to let's switch it to a loop agent. As you can see, the main thing that I'm highlighting over here is the max iterations. These are the bounded retries that we have added. If there are any sort of failures happening, the agentic workflow will ensure to retry. Right now, you can see there are multiple sub-agents over here, like data gathering agent, synthesis agent, grounding agent. We add an iteration for the entire loop. This might be not that cost efficient, but maybe we can add this max iteration to a particular agent as well where the main work is handled. In this case, I'm showing the entire agent can make sure the workflow is computed properly, so that the output is saved and you can increase the number of iterations as much as you want. Like here, I've just given as an example of five iterations.

Next one, so we were flying blind. Observability is a must. This is a very important thing. Since we had full chain available, the very common thing that we want to ensure is we should have observability in the entire workflow. What do I mean by that? The regular way of doing the engineering is you can have maybe 5xx errors or 4xx errors. Even here it's the same case, like if we saw like there's a schema violation, or if there are retries that didn't happen, or something that went wrong, we were adding structured logging. Structured logging was ensured. Over here you can see, as an example, is how many times the retries happened, like two attempts. Or if there was a schema violation, how much latency it had. All of this was enabled just to make sure that we have clear visibility into what's happening in our entire workflow.

As you can see over here, we had proper logging if the LLM response doesn't match the schema, if there is a tool response that failed, so it was retrying again. We were trying to reach a success rate of 99%, so this is some example that I added, like if there's a 97% error rate, 2.3% of failure rate, and so on. We made sure that observability is also in place.

That being said, these were the four main failures. Now I want to get to the very crisp part of what we were building over here. With failures behind us, the next question on the table was cost. This was the biggest question that was running on to us, because we wanted to get this into production. This was a very critical thing that we were trying to get in, but we were leveraging all foundational models, and with a high scale, like 4700 stores, the amount of tokens generated is quite high. How much of this whole solution is going to cost to run, is what was the next question. The thing over here is the PTU problem. When the solution went to production, we had humongous amount of input and output tokens being used. Since it was a foundational model, we decided to secure 400 PTUs for that amount of scale that we need to run.

For 400 PTUs, we were almost being charged around 100k to 120k per month, and the solution was not that, because we are trying to also make sure that the inventory is accurate, also save cost. There should not be wastage happening in a particular department. Running at this position, it doesn't make sense, if these much PTUs are going to be used. PTUs is like reserved capacity, and we have to reserve it for the entire day. Any of these vendors who are providing the PTUs, we have to take it for the entire 24 hours, and it's a monthly or yearly subscription that we have to take in. Now the problem is, this is a batch intelligence application, it's only going to run overnight. It's not going to run the entire day. We are not serving any live traffic. For us, we were being charged 400 PTUs for 24 hours, and PTUs reserve capacity for the entire day.

Our workload was nightly batch run, which was not 24 by 7. We were paying for the round the clock capacity which was being used. This was our most critical problem that we were trying to solve in a particular defined set of time, which didn't make sense because of the cost involved. We started exploring options, what are the options? Because this is a foundational model, the best part about foundational model is they are well trained, they are good for such enterprise scale applications. The next thing that came to us was, what AI model should I choose? Here as you can see, we had cheaper models where we can go with open-source models or any other models, which might introduce some latency, or they could be cheaper compared to the one which we already had, whether it's a GPT-4.1 or Gemini, and so on. Or we can just reduce the PTUs, that was another option. Or we could go with pay-as-you-go. We were debating between quality versus cost, and both were not a good option, because we needed high quality but lower cost. That was the main problem that we had to solve.

How did we do that? The decision that we made was, we went with pay-as-you-go. Now just to go with some background, the problem with PTU versus pay-as-you-go, is pay-as-you-go will come with latency issues, as I've mentioned over here, and there will be rate limiting happening. We did observe a lot of rate limit issues, but now the thing is, as I mentioned in my failures as well, we had added a retry logic. This retry logic enabled us, even if there is a rate limit, if there are any 4xx or 5xx errors, I'm just going to retry again. If I do retry again, the output will be generated again. Now, if it's a pay-as-you-go, it's still a foundational model and it still gives very accurate responses, and there was no reserved capacity as well over here. We were not paying round the clock, we were just using as much compute as we require.

The payoff, so what happened over here is, we were supposed to pay around 100k per month, now we are paying just 10k as the final usage, because even with the retries, the cost is just very low. It's just going to happen in that specific 30 minutes, or maybe the time might increase. We don't mind because the stores are already closed, this is going to be a nightly job. Then, eventually, whatever compute is being taken is going to just happen at night, even if there are retries and everything, the cost will be minimal, output will be still matching the quality that we have set, because there is schema enforcement, and all the data engineering pipelines were fixed. This was our biggest win. As I mentioned, same tokens, same model, just a pricing tier switch from PTU to pay-as-you-go, and for a drastic drop in cost. That was the big win that I wanted to mention over here.

Every failure and every fix left us with a lesson worth carrying forward. Here's what we learned, building at scale. These are some of the learnings that I'm going to mention once again. Basically, schema enforcement. Since we are retrying, everything is all planned out, but schema enforcement is not just the one thing that happens over here, basic JSON validation. There has to be semantic validation, because data, what is coming from various sources, like in the AI domain, what I've learned very well is context has to be very accurate. With the data pipelines that we have, whatever context we get, if there is even a slight mismatch, it can just return vague output. We have to make sure semantic validation is in place. Data usability, making data easy to understand and use. We need to have some observability as well. Whatever the data that is coming in, we need to see how the pipelines are running.

All those things have to be taken into consideration. Then comes the data integrity. Maintaining accuracy and consistency of data is very important, is what I've learned from this entire perspective. That's one of the key features. Second thing is data engineering limits AI quality. As I mentioned over here, data quality over here is reliable AI results, accurate and trustworthy outcomes, data rectification, fixing upstream data issues, data engineering, ensuring data quality, and flawed data. What do we mean by all of this? The entire context over here, since it was a nightly job that was being run, this had a huge emphasis on the data engineering aspects itself. Because we were getting data from various sources, there was a lot of focus that was added into this perspective, where data coming from various sources has to be verified. The amount of scripts that we created were validated with the business and the data team, with the engineering team.

We ensured that once the data is very accurate, then that context will be fed properly to the agents with a proper particular prompt, and that will generate the exact output that we are looking for. Because it's a multi-agent workflow, we have to ensure that the data that is coming from various sources has to be very accurate. That was our main goal that we learned from this entire workflow. Also, like flawed data, as I mentioned, unreliable input is also like, once the input is not proper, all the agents will react in a weird output, because it might either not match to the schema, or it might just match to the schema also, but just generate vague outputs, and that's how it would return. Building retry logic, this was one of the most important aspects that I went through. We have been very much emphasizing on this.

Retries can be a very bad loop as well, where if you don't plan it properly, it can just keep retrying, and that would just increase a lot of costs. Just because there are tokens involved over here, you have to plan it very accurately. As I mentioned in the initial flow, we used to retry it at the base, like root level, where all the agents are, like where the workflow runs. Ideally, the agentic retry should be in such a pattern where it is actually needed, whether we are getting the context from the proper data source, so that the further agents don't have to hallucinate, or there could be something that can go wrong. Retry over here, implemented from the outset, reduced unexpected failures. There's proactive system enhancement, cost saving and efficiency. It results into better user satisfaction.

The next learning perspective is observability. This is one of the key things from the entire workflow, that everyone is focused on. Traceability is important, structured logging is important, and enhanced system understanding. Because once you have tracing enabled, for us, initially, when we were having this entire workflow running, we were not able to determine, ok, what's going wrong, just because there are no proper traces set up. If you're not able to identify if the LLM is hallucinating, or if the model is just getting rate limited, all that has to be clearly available. There are tools which help us add those visibility, and then having that in place, make sure that your application is very robust, and can survive any failures to make it very resilient. That's a very important aspect that I'll mention over here. The next thing is matching infrastructure to requirements. This is the key thing that we realized, which is the infrastructure should be used for a nightly batch job.

Here, we can see that the real-time infrastructure, like if you have a real-time infrastructure where users are having conversations with the LLM, in that case, you can have an accurate set of PTUs set up, and so on. In cost effective infrastructures, you need to ensure that you don't need to actually have PTUs only allocated. Here, in our case, we were opting either for like pay-as-you-go, or you can even go with open-source models. As long as it's giving you the proper performance, the correct output, that's the ideal approach that you should be going with. The next one is, I've reached the end, which is, tomorrow at 6 a.m., a store manager will confidently adjust the inventory. They don't know about our schema validation, our loop retries, our nightly API optimizations. They don't have to as well. It's just the ultimate metric, which is the resilient engineering. That's what the perspective is.

Just to recap over here, schema is our table stakes, semantics is the real work. Focus on validation checks that go beyond basic JSON structure. Data engineering limits AI quality, so garbage in results into garbage out as well. Having retry logic is very important. If there are network timeouts, hallucinations, retry can ensure that your output is always accurate. Observability is mandatory. Tracing, logging is very important. Then match infrastructure to the regular requirements. If it's a nightly non-latency sensitive batch job, then you have to ensure that you don't need to actually rely on PTUs, because that would just cost you even more than what's expected. That's the main goal.

#9777. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#9775. Amutable Foundations: A Technical Overview

The image-based OS approach enables us to enforce some very strict but powerful security properties, which elevate the security posture of the system substantially above traditional Linux systems. Specifically, let's highlight seven major essential security properties of AOS here: No Shell + No SSH + No Language Interpreters. By default AOS does not install a UNIX shell, nor makes remote access via SSH available on the nodes. Moreover, we do not install any of the usual language interpreters (Python, Perl, …) by default. For most nodes a shell or interpreted language support is not required and it removes a whole class of attacks. Signed Images Only. On AOS only images that come with Verity data signed by a signing key listed in the Verity keyring may be activated. #9774. US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

Erroneous or outdated DNS records can give attackers surprising powers over organizations' email systems.

Simple oversights in domain name system (DNS) records are exposing government organizations to all kinds of potential impersonation, spying, and more.

In a new study of more than 25,000 government-related domains, SH Consulting founder Alex Shakhov found dozens whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. Though few in number, those vulnerable included all sorts of agencies representing US towns, cities, counties, regulatory boards, and more.

Many of the erroneous records pointed to domains that were either available to, or already snapped up by, attackers. Depending on the nature of the error, they could allow attackers to send or receive email on behalf of vulnerable government agencies, reconfigure their DNS records, read their security records, and more.

"Typos in DNS are very dangerous, because technically the organization is being hacked without anyone breaking into its systems," Shakhov tells Dark Reading. "You already have a domain with a reputation established over years. You put whatever IPs you want into DNS, spin up an email server, and send emails out, exploiting that reputation and users' trust. And these attacks are very difficult to detect, because the attackers didn't break anything. They just registered a domain sitting in the DNS that nobody knew existed."

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

After Dark Reading ran this story, Livingston County, Mich., the city of Waynesboro, Tenn., and the Alabama legislature have all implemented or begun working on fixes for their DNS vulnerabilities.

Little matters more to a website's security than its DNS records, which include instructions about where the website lives in IP space (A/AAAA), its domain (CNAME), how its email is handled (MX, TXT), and who decides these details in the first place (NS). At the end of the day, though, it's a totally public set of information in plaintext. A simple typo in any of these instructions can have surprisingly significant impacts.

Take Livingston County, Mich., and the city of Pikeville, Ky. These two government bodies seem to have authorized Amazon's Simple Email Service (SES) for its day-to-day email needs and, as such, their TXT records specify it as a trusted third-party provider. The domains they list, however, contain typos: "amzonses[.]com" and "amasonses[.]com." Thanks to these mistakes, these bodies have been allowing a non-Amazon entity to send emails on their behalf.

To what end? When Shakhov checked the two organizations' Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allowlists, he found that Pikeville's listed 75 IP addresses, and Livingston's listed more than 32,000 different IP addresses, all authorized to send mail on behalf of their official domains. As a result, Pikeville's official government domain is now listed on the URI blacklist website "URIBL," and Shakhov assessed that "it's reasonable to assume the domain is still being used for abuse."

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

In the Livingston County case, the "included" SPF list was rotated every three to eight days since 2021. This suggested that an attacker was performing a "snowshoe" operation: switching to new sending IPs, sending unwanted or malicious emails, and once those IPs attained bad reputations, cycling in new ones.

This information alone doesn't necessarily prove that attackers were abusing Livingston County's email domain, or prove how much they might have. But it does prove that they could have. Shakhov connected the actor behind this compromise to a previously documented group that was seen abusing websites from major corporations such as Oracle and CNN Money as well as universities — like the Universities of California in Los Angeles, Davis, San Diego, and Santa Cruz (UCLA, UC Davis, UC San Diego, and UC Santa Cruz) — and the Connecticut state government, thanks to expired CNAME records.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Just about any DNS record can be abused if it contains a typo or refers to an otherwise incorrect domain for some other reason. The nature of the abuse depends, however, on the record in question. Once they register a so-called "dangling" (purchasable) domain, attackers can intercept mail (if the issue lies with an MX record), serve spam content (if it's in CNAME or NS), send phishing that appears to come from a legitimate sender (SPF), or collect security intel through Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC).

For example, the website for the City of Rupert, Idaho, currently refers to its neighbor Heyburn's old domain name, heyburnidaho[.]org. That domain was purchased by a malicious actor, which reworked its name server (NS) records to point to its shady gambling website. The actor also arranged to be able to send and receive emails from addresses with an @heyburnidaho.org suffix.

A less serious exposure could occur if attackers grab hold of a DMARC reporting domain. DMARC is an email security protocol, and its part of a TXT record can tell a mail server where to send reports. Those reports can contain sensitive information about an organization's email infrastructure. Shakhov found 11 local government institutions at risk of this sort of information theft, including four county and law enforcement agencies from Jennings County, Ind.

Taking advantage of these situations is one of the easiest jobs hackers can choose for themselves. "Attackers constantly scan DNS records for vulnerabilities and mistyped domains, because it's one of the easiest and cheapest ways to get into someone's infrastructure," Shakhov explains.

"Records at the root domain, like MX, NS, SPF, DMARC, CAA, etc., can be looked up by anyone," he continues. "Subdomains are harder to find, but Certificate Transparency logs reveal most of them. So attackers just scan DNS in bulk and get whatever they want. It's even easier for government domains, because it’s only about 26,000 domains to scan, and attackers can do it multiple times a day at almost no cost. CISA even publishes the full list of .gov domains, so attackers don't have to find them."

Shakhov laments that while DNS has been around for nearly half a century, "There's typically no one at an organization responsible for DNS management. As a result, over time it often turns into a graveyard of expired domains from previous vendors, former corporate domains forgotten after acquisitions and mergers, or just typos, when someone typed a record by hand instead of copying and pasting it."

Proper DNS hygiene, he says, requires that organizations follow at least a few core processes. First of all, he argues, "Admins and IT teams must stop typing DNS records by hand. Across millions of domains we scanned this year, 47% of the unregistered domains we found in SPF and DMARC records were typos, either of the organization's own domain or of a provider's."

Second, organizations must have a map of their DNS infrastructure and know where every DNS record came from. Depending on the circumstances, this can be easier said than done. "At universities, it's quite common for students to put a project on GitHub and ask the IT team to add a CNAME so it lives under the university domain," Shakhov explains. "The student graduates, but the CNAME stays. The GitHub account gets abandoned and removed, so whoever creates an account with the same name already has a CNAME sitting under the university's DNS."

Organizations should also consider registering misspelled versions of their own domains to prevent attackers from snapping them up later.

And, finally, "Regular DNS audits are a must," Shakhov says. "In most cases, it's just a simple script that scans your DNS for invalid domains or destinations and flags them. It's never been that difficult to do a quarterly DNS review to make sure everything is up to date."

This story was updated at 3:05 p.m. ET on Nov. 10 to reflect actions by multiple US government agencies to address their DNS vulnerabilities.

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9773. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

#9772. Asahi Linux 7.3 progress report

Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors. As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only. Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it.
