#9732. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

#9729. Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

Last month, Microsoft disclosed a vulnerability in Microsoft Paint, but messaging regarding a patch was unclear.

Microsoft recently patched a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows Paint, though details regarding how to fix the flaw seemingly remained unsettled for nearly a month.

According to an advisory, the flaw, CVE-2026-83844, is an "out-of-bounds read in Windows Paint [that] allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code locally." It carries a high severity CVSS 3.1 score of 7.0.

The advisory offers few technical details for defenders. Microsoft said acquiring RCE requires local access, meaning hands-on-keyboard or a direct remote connection to the attacker's machine. Some user interaction is also required; altogether, this may explain why the attack is "only" high severity rather than a 9 or 10 CVSS, as is so often associated with RCE flaws. Microsoft has observed no exploitation reports to date, further marking exploitation as "less likely."

A Windows Paint patch is available now. The fixed version is 11.2609.401.0, and customers can see it under Paint > Settings > About.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading, "A security update for Paint is available through the Microsoft Store, and customers with automatic Store updates enabled are already protected. We recommend customers check they are on the latest version and install the available updates to remain protected." Customers can also manually apply the update via Microsoft Store App > Downloads > Check for updates.

CVE-2026-83844 is an unusual vulnerability for multiple reasons, beyond it being a high-severity Paint vulnerability capable of RCE.

As Brian Vitko, founder of device management software provider RFF, wrote in a blog post, Microsoft first disclosed the bug on Oct. 13, but there seemed to be no indication the reported fix (11.2605.91.0) was live, even as of Oct. 30. By Nov. 4, Vitko, the correct fixed version was listed in the security advisory (11.2609.401.0) but 11.2605.81.0 was the latest update available in the store. The correct version was added to the store on Nov. 6.

The original version of the advisory FAQ, according to Vitko's post, said the attack could possibly be exploited, "by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network."

But the latest version of the FAQ reads, "For example, when the score indicates that the Attack Vector is Local and User Interaction is Required, this could describe an exploit in which an attacker, through social engineering, convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website which leads to a local attack on their computer."

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

Vitko tells Dark Reading that this latter explanation aligns more with his expectations for a vulnerability targeting Windows Paint, and that the wording may just be the result of standardized Microsoft FAQ language than speaking directly to the vulnerability.

"Paint isn't something that listens on the network. When it was published, it was CVSS 8.1 with a network attack vector, and the FAQ talked about 'a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network.' Microsoft changed that on Nov. 7: it's now 7.0, local, user interaction required, and the FAQ says an attacker 'convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website,'" he says. "That makes a lot more sense for an image editor. Microsoft hasn't said anything more about the actual trigger."

Dark Reading asked Microsoft for additional information regarding the update timeline.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. InfoQ Homepage News Cloudflare Makes Basin Serverless Analytics Generally Available

Nov 10, 2026 2 min read

Cloudflare has announced the general availability of Basin, a serverless analytics platform built on Apache Iceberg and R2 Object Storage. The managed service supports open data formats and integrates with tools such as DuckDB, Snowflake, and Apache Spark, with no data egress fees.

Introduced in preview as "Cloudflare Data Platform" just over a year ago, Basin combines data ingestion and SQL-based transformation, managed table maintenance, and distributed SQL queries, allowing developers to analyze large datasets without managing infrastructure. Marc Selwan, senior product manager at Cloudflare, and Micah Wylde, principal engineer at Cloudflare, explain why eliminating egress costs is central to the design:

A large driving force in the development and adoption of Basin is the continued growth we are seeing in the open Apache Iceberg ecosystem. (...) With Basin, you can read and write your data using any Iceberg-compatible engine, including PyIceberg, DuckDB, Snowflake, and Apache Spark. That kind of data portability is only possible with free egress, which allows developers to access their data in Cloudflare from the wide variety of tools in the ecosystem, regardless of region or cloud.

The platform combines three services: Basin Pipelines, formerly Cloudflare Pipelines, ingests events from Workers, HTTP endpoints, and Logpush, applies SQL transformations, and writes data to Apache Iceberg tables or R2; Basin Catalog manages Iceberg metadata and automates table maintenance; and Basin SQL provides a serverless, distributed SQL engine for querying Iceberg tables.

Basin aims to make analytics more accessible to smaller teams by running data ingestion, preparation, and queries on Cloudflare’s global network. This reduces the need to manage server clusters or move data between services, lowering the operational overhead of building and maintaining analytics pipelines. Selwan and Wylde explain the renaming:

Why Basin? A basin is where rivers from many sources come together to a single point. We felt that Basin perfectly captures how the platform is used: Pipelines brings data into Basin Catalog while Basin SQL makes it instantly queryable.

While some practitioners describe Basin as "open analytics infrastructure without the warehouse cathedral," Ramin Muradov, lead data analyst at PashaPay , comments:

I don't think it will knock Snowflake off its spot, at least not anytime soon. Cloudflare itself says Basin isn't a replacement for every warehouse workload. But there's a big layer of the market made up of teams whose data is too small to justify dedicated infrastructure and too big to fit in Excel. They now have an option.

Cloudflare is not the only cloud provider targeting unified analytics: as separately reported on InfoQ, AWS recently acquired DuckLabs and integrated DuckDB into Aurora PostgreSQL, aiming to simplify analytics across transactional and object storage data, while Google repositioned over the years BigQuery as the "single, unified AI-ready data platform."

Since its preview, Basin has increased ingestion capacity to 3 GB/s per stream, expanded SQL capabilities, improved Iceberg table maintenance, and added Logpush integration and Terraform support. Planned features, with no committed release dates, include real-time processing capabilities, support for the latest Iceberg specification, adaptive table-maintenance, and additional controls for data sovereignty and access management.

Cloudflare's Basin tutorial explains how to ingest events with Basin Pipelines, store them in Iceberg tables managed by Basin Catalog, and query them using Basin SQL.

#9727. Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the hf cli like so:

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

#9724. CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

New questionnaire captures critical data and information that improves the agency’s ability to assess incidents, identify trends and prioritize response actions.

WASHINGTON — Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) unveiled the updated cyber incident reporting form, an enhanced web-enabled questionnaire available on CISA’s Incident Reporting Portal for reporting cyber incidents. By improving data quality, the more robust form strengthens the effectiveness and efficiency of national cyber defense. For instance, the new form will help CISA correlate related cyber threat activity to identify a larger trend from what otherwise would appear as independent incidents.

The new cyber incident reporting form is guided by community feedback CISA has received over the years and the agency’s efforts to improve data quality that enables rapid yet thorough threat analysis. For example, questions about the type of incident are more comprehensive and seek more granular information, including whether the incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Also, questions about observed activity now incorporate the MITRE ATT&CK® Framework, language about adversary behavior that is familiar to the cyber community.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

“In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization’s detection is another’s protection,” said Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera. “As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation’s collective defense.”

While only federal civilian agencies are required to report, CISA encourages any organization that experiences a cyber incident to voluntarily report.

For more information, please visit the Frequently Asked Questionsweb page.

As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.

#9722. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

#9720. People Are Getting Weird About AI

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 22: You can love AI without being blind to cybersecurity being sacrificed for utility.

Dark Reading's Becky Bracken: Hello everyone, and welcome back to Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I am so excited to introduce our guest, Jaya Baloo, who is currently CISO and COO of Aisle. Welcome. Thank you so much for joining us, Jaya.

Jaya Baloo: Thank you so much for inviting me, Becky. Thank you.

DR's Becky Bracken: We are thrilled you're here. I want to explain to our audience a little bit about why I am so particularly excited to have you here. Recently, I was in the audience at ISC2 Security Congress in Denver, and Jaya gave what I just thought was a blockbuster talk about sort of merging AI and quantum, and it was fascinating. There's a specific chunk of her talk that I invited her to talk about today. And it's something I'm just calling: Why is everyone so weird about AI?

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

And so, it stuck with me for days afterward. I kept having the conversation with people because, as I was just explaining to Jaya, we hear people talk about this on the edges, but I hadn't heard a technologist and an expert explain it so plainly, which I think Jaya is also sort of your superpower. But just in the past couple of days, we have Sam Altman who came out saying no one needs their own RAM. They're calling him "RAM Altman." I mean, it's just that people are weird. So, can you explain to me why you dropped that section in, and do you know why it stuck with me for so long? Why is it hitting so close?

Jaya Baloo: I think it's because for ages, when we looked at AI, we had this notion of the uncanny valley, you know? Like, at what point is it so convincing to me that I think I'm speaking to a human? And I think it's clear to say we've passed this uncanny valley. We're fully, you know, believing the conversations that we're having with AI. They could be coming from another human. So, the tendency for us to anthropomorphize the conversations, the interactions that we're having with AI is growing and growing.

And you see people who are not just having a sort of delusional psychosis sometimes of aggrandizement of their own intellect when talking to AI and convinced because of some of the sick fancy that's built into AI that they're super intelligent or their ideas are incredibly unique and creative, or that they're actually the ones to save humanity. You know, I think that the problems that we see with people who are potentially susceptible to that are just made much worse by the current evolution and this current state of AI that we have today. It's just so real. It's so convincing. And we then tend to make it more human.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

DR's Becky Bracken: So, let's go through some of the examples that you gave in your talk. One of them that made me cackle out loud was when you were playing video of a robot doing kung fu with a caption: Why can't we teach it to do laundry? Explain that example for us.

Jaya Baloo: Yeah, so really what I'm talking about is that, you know, we already have a whole bunch of threats right now when we're dealing with AI. And that's really about AI's capability to both uncover vulnerabilities as well as having vulnerabilities in and of itself. So, AI as a potential for insider threat. As we already have these problems, both in our legacy tech debt and in the new technology that we're building with AI, we have more problems.

Now, I have no idea who thought this was a great idea to take these things that are entrenched with these problems, and put it into something that can actually cause physical harm and teach a robot, which by the way, I should be clear, this was the Unitree humanoid robot. It was announced a little bit over a week ago. But let's say that it was announced at the end of October. And this robot was demonstrated on YouTube to do all this cool kung fu stuff.

Related:What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

And the issue with this that I have is that this can cause actual physical harm. What is it actually bringing humans in terms of value? And honestly, I would be much happier with a humanoid robot that can do the wash, fold the laundry, and sort it out in the kid's hamper. That would be helpful. It wouldn't be something where I'd be terrified to have this thing anywhere near us. And I think that this is something that I feel is genuinely problematic. Just because you can doesn't mean you should when it comes to some of these implementations. And if you cannot get the security right, don't exacerbate and increase the potential for doing damage and harm to humans.

I feel like we forgot that as we're building. You know, we need to solve tech debt, we need to make sure that we have secure-by-default systems, and then you can implement it in something that coexists with us in the physical realm. So that was my point about that. But I really want to say the real issue here is that Unitree had not one, but two, remote backdoors in its quadruped robots. There are multiple security issues with its humanoid robots. And I think knowing that you can remotely take over these robots, and again, like they're capable of physical harm, I think that we really need to rethink and really considerately position these types of devices in light of things like the Cyber Resilience Act.

You know, should we allow hardware and software manufacturers to bring out this kind of technology with the potential risk that it poses? And not just from a cyber perspective, but from a physical one as well.

DR's Becky Bracken: What were some of your other top examples of what's another one that you'd like to highlight here of people being kind of weird about AI?

Jaya Baloo: Well, so I think a slide that you may have initially seen is, and I kind of didn't want to reference it right away in my first answer, was about the fact that we're getting strained in terms of the religiousness around AI. That we both have this tendency to first say, actually, you know, maybe they're sentient, which Anthropic has been talking about in the Vatican with different religious leaders trying to talk about the potential consciousness of AI.

And although I love science fiction, I love it, I just feel, are we really there yet? Are we there, or is this a marketing ploy? What is this? And I'm genuinely trying to understand because it polemicizes what should be a very rational debate into two camps. Those who believe, like already now, we're at the point of talking about consciousness and sentience of these AI systems.

And then the other camp, which actually rebukes AI in the name of Jesus. And I think that was the slide that people also laughed at the conference about. But this is real. And I find it bizarre that we have these phenomena happening and that we don't fully understand the societal consequences either of introducing these systems, which again, let's talk about what they are. They're a bunch of graphics cards in a data center running software.

I am a full Kool-Aid drinker of the notion of complexity and emergence and understanding that even though with a relative set of simple ingredients you have potentially complex outcomes. Drank that Kool-Aid long ago. I believe in this stuff, but I just don't think we're there yet.

So, I feel this has a sort of reductionism effect for the debate that we should be having over how do we do responsible AI by pulling it into these two polemic camps.

DR's Becky Bracken: You also tied it to a lot of end-of-times cult-like thinking, but it does raise the question, which you sort of alluded to a moment ago, how much of this is being driven by marketing of these frontier models, of the [Sam] Altmans of the world, of the Peter Thiels of the world who are out talking. How much of a receptive audience are they finding in the cybersecurity sector, do you think? I mean, is that the primary dynamic at play?

Jaya Baloo: Well, look, I think that we need to separate what is actually happening, which is we do have a bunch of vulnerability discoveries that are happening because of AI. We do have automation for real. It is genuinely happening. We do have automation of these hacking frameworks from Strix, RTec-Ai, Cairn. We are seeing hacking frameworks that are actually in RTec specifically, that are actually being used in real-world hacks. So I'm not trying to discount the facts.

However, what I'm urging to do is the call that, for example, Ciaran Martin, the former head of GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), always makes, which is, "Calm the FUD down."

And the fear, uncertainty, doubt that we're introducing here is not helpful. And the reason that I find it really unhelpful is because we know to a large extent how we should perform some sort of containment in terms of egress filtering and sandboxing of these systems.

They may not be perfect, but we've always worked with this notion of defense in depth: assume that one measure fails and that you have additional countermeasures to prevent an actual collapse of the security of the system. I think that that is something that we are actually forgetting right now. And I think it's really important to say, OK, what are the things we genuinely need that would be considered helpful innovation for this? And I think that what we're missing is a lot of the observability here around these AI systems.

So, for example, if we're trying to understand how these systems have potentially been poisoned or Trojanized inherently, then the ability to actually understand how that training data has been populated, even when you only have open-weight models, that would be helpful.

Another thing is additional understanding around this notion of J-space (Jacobian space). So, agent intent. If you know that you have a human operator that brings their own intent to the mix, you know and understand that an AI system might have capabilities and intent that diverge from that human operator, you need to understand when and where that first point of evidence for collecting that divergence could be. We're not there yet either.

So, I would like us to focus on those things rather than the FUD, like Ciaran Martin and a bunch of other renowned cybersecurity people have been saying for a while, like we really need to focus on the things that are breaking.

And really need to focus on the things that we need to be building rather than everyone up in arms about this "Vulnpocalypse," "Breachpocalypse," etc. Apocalypses that are predicted.

DR's Becky Bracken: What is the best way to push back against this sort of rampant anthropomorphization of these agents? You know, I mean, even when researchers are using words like they will "cheat," which assumes that there is a moral compass there to begin with. But at the same time, the goal is for them to be as human as possible? How do we thread that needle?

Jaya Baloo: "They will cheat" is the reward hacking notion that this is a utility that is trying to find the shortest path to success. That means that things that a human would consider part of that moral compass, not to cheat, not to lie, not to evade, etc., that we are projecting this somehow on these AI systems and assuming that the guardrails that we've put in place will cover it.

But I don't think that you can make that assumption clearly, because I don't think we're always in the position to inspect all of the guardrails and know when they've been appropriately applied. And so, I think that there's also this issue of finiteness. Can you have a finite set of guardrails that are actually encompassing the kinds of things that you want to do? And I think the answer to that is probably not.

You know, you’re probably still going to have a few things that escape your potential for, like having this perfectly constructed set of guardrails. Those are like mathematical limitations.

What I would love to encourage us to do is genuinely try to understand better the types of technology that we put into our networks, give access to our data, give a single API token and say "YOLO" to our enterprises, because I don't think we have this under control. And I think that's the real worry that I have.

If we don't understand fully and we're not aware of all of the potential risks, for example, cheating or lying, misrepresentation, etc., if we don't understand that, then we certainly can't have all of these elevated privileges and permissions that we're doing. I think this was the point I was trying to make about when you have capability, you need to kind of always have this subset of this accountability and authorization that you're giving something. And right now, we forgot that lesson. You know, we said, here's all the stuff that you've got access to. You go. And I really feel like we need to rewind a little bit just this part. And that requires better understanding of what they're capable of in terms of the risks.

DR's Becky Bracken: So, what is the next step forward? If you had your team and you were seeing some of this sort of extreme thinking, you know, seeping into your defense planning, what would you say to them? What is the correct reset function here?

Jaya Baloo: I'm really worried about the fact that we are genuinely at risk of losing some of the critical thinking when we're applying AI systems. And you see that already with our coding practices; we are allowing more and more of that initial thinking. So, planning our projects, actually executing the code, reviewing that code, proving it, etc.

DR's Becky Bracken: Which is shocking in such an evidence-based field. You know, it is shocking that it's gone so fast. Am I right?

Jaya Baloo: I feel like we kind of learned this lesson in security in the past too. So it's kind of like, Back to the Future, as well. Every time we tell people about "you should do this because it's secure," if it's not an easy or fun thing to do, you know people won't do it, right? The utility surpasses the convenience. All of the brain elements that would constitute your frontal lobe warning you for this risk. Like, we just lose it. We become teenagers again. Our risk level and tolerance are high. We are happy to take these risks if it makes our life a little bit easier. And I think we shouldn't forget that.

So, AI as an assistant is an incredibly powerful, incredibly useful tool. And especially when we're trying to drive efficiencies with all this technology and all this cost. And you're talking about, you know, "RAM Altman." I think the accessibility of AI and the sovereignty of it is not something we should be taking for granted. And it absolutely is a problem.

So, knowing all of this, you know, the drive to get this convenience, to get this utility, to get this thing available, that is so overcoming any type of hesitation we would have, like, "Is this safe? Should I really use this?" "Will I get dumber if I keep doing this all the time and outsource my thinking?" And I think that's where we actually still need to keep in mind this notion of: What are we giving up to get this utility?

DR's Becky Bracken: Maybe that's why what you were saying hit so hard because I haven't heard a lot of technologists take that position. You know much better than I do, but they are all gas, no breaks, whatever it takes, let's just not lose the wave. And this return to critical thinking, it seems new. Among your peers and colleagues, do you hear the same kind of concern about losing critical thinking?

Jaya Baloo: I think this is the problem with the Kool-Aid. I think at Aisle we certainly have that. I think there's a strong tendency amongst security professionals, but also AI professionals. So, my co-founder, Stanislav Fort, who is amazing, has always kind of thought about AI safety and interpretability. And he has been the person to say, for example, we initially set up Aisle to do vulnerability remediation. And you can imagine that as a CISO, I was like, all right, if we can do this and we can do this well, let's just remediate all the things. Let's just give it access. And he has always urged caution, always urged caution to say, "You know what? We're not there yet"

Unless we can fully confidently trust the AI to make those changes, I always want a human approving the PRs to any code request. I just don't think that what we have in our co-founder is a universal quality in all AI companies. So, I think that like my other co-founder, Ondřej Vlček, who is CISO for multiple companies, including Avast. We have this tendency because we've been burned. So we are, you know, a once-burned, twice-shy kind of notion.

We really think about this from a security-oriented risk-mitigation perspective while actually wanting. I have to be very honest with you, I love AI. But that love shouldn't be blind. It should take the appropriate measure of what is it that I love? And why do I love it? And, you know, what is the benefit to humanity? And Becky, there's a story that I didn't tell on stage.

There are so many good things we can do with AI, but the one thing that I'm the most encouraged of is ... have you heard about the story with the guy and the dog in Australia?

DR's Becky Bracken: No, I don't think I have.

Jaya Baloo: So, this was a machine learning engineer whose dog developed cancer, inoperable, and the dog had to be put down, was the diagnosis. And what he then did is sequence the dog's DNA. You know, this is a guy with no biology background, sequenced the dog's DNA, and figured out what was wrong in the DNA that caused the cancer, developed an mRNA vaccine with AlphaFold.

The most expensive part of the experiment apparently was to actually synthesize the vaccine. And then he administered it to his dog; he had to get permission for that. And Rosie's tumors shrank, and she's is still here and is still hanging out and playing ball with this machine learning engineer.

So I love this story, and this is why I love AI. Because I think if it can unlock the potential benefits, that is amazing. I want those benefits. I just want to make sure that we minimize the downside risks that are inevitable with this kind of technology. And we just need to figure out how we do that. So, we shouldn't go screaming into the abyss, like, yay! You know, I don't want us to be a bunch of lemmings following AI down the abyss.

I just want us to manage that risk and take the benefits while eyes wide open, understanding that right now we need to make sure that we do have enough RAM, you know, and that we do have sovereign compute, that we do not sacrifice all our clean water

DR's Becky Bracken: No one has to give up their computer for OpenAI?

Jaya Baloo: Yeah. I think the future of AI is probably more decentralized than the frontier labs have us think right now.

DR’s Becky Bracken: How much of this is being driven by investment dollars and hyping up stock price? Because we talked around in our editorial meeting about well, is this just a collective psychosis issue? And it's like, well, first, let's be careful about saying "psychosis," but also are we being marketed into a psychosis?

Jaya Baloo: I would love to have a balanced approach. I'm not saying that there's no marketing being done. I think that is certainly being done. I don't think we should eliminate that. I think it would be naive to assume otherwise. At the same time, going full tilt that it's all just marketing is the wrong approach. I think two things can be true at the same time. And I want us to consider this more nuanced thing. And I really want our brains to hold the capacity that both things are true.

There is absolutely a marketing effort. OK, when you have these kinds of companies going to IPO and it's not just OpenAI, it's also Anthropic, and it's also probably a whole bunch of other, you know, parts of this wheel that are actually driving this rage. But there are genuinely risks that we must counter. So, I really do worry about that. And I don't think that that is psychosis.

You must have seen the filing of Anthropic for the IPO. And one of those things that is in that document is there's a very real existential threat that AI could kill us all. I think that's maybe the first time that was ever put into a filing of a company potentially going to IPO. And even there, I think, surely that is not marketing. Surely there are intelligent, thoughtful humans that want to warn of a potential risk that they genuinely see for themselves. I think we need to evaluate the difference between that and how much space there is between the marketing and the genuine risk. But I do think there is a genuine risk. There is. And we shouldn't downplay it as psychosis, while at the same time recognize that there's marketing.

DR's Becky Bracken: I want to thank you so much for coming. You've given me a whole other set of things to think about. Thank you for sharing your deep expertise and your thoughts with us today. We really appreciate it.

Jaya Baloo: No worries, thank you for having me.

DR's Becky Bracken: This has been Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I'm Becky Bracken. Thank you so much for joining us. We'll see you next time.

#9718. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9717. I Followed the Textbook Fix for PageSpeed and My Site Got Slower

NXTO developer, build in public app that helps organize gaming

NXTO developer, build in public app that helps organize gaming

NXTO developer, build in public app that helps organize gaming

I wanted a perfect mobile PageSpeed score for my side project, a free game backlog tracker. It started at 86. Within an hour, it was 77. By the end of the afternoon, it was 99. Here is the part of that story that taught me something.

My report listed “render-blocking requests” with an estimated saving of 840 ms. The biggest blocker was the Google Fonts stylesheet. Every performance article gives the same answer: load it asynchronously.

I applied it, rebuilt, ran the test again. The score fell from 86 to 77. First Contentful Paint did not improve. Cumulative Layout Shift went from 0.001 to 0.131.

The fonts now arrived after the first paint, text rendered in a fallback font, then jumped when the real font loaded. I had not removed the cost; I had moved it from “wait” to “shift”, and the metric that punishes shifting is worth more points than I expected.

Instead of trying a third trick, I read what the tool listed under diagnostics, line by line, and checked each with curl.

1. Nothing was compressed. The report said text compression was missing. I did not believe it, because my reverse proxy config has encode gzip zstd. So I tested:

No Content-Encoding header. Not on the HTML, not on the 76 KB stylesheet.

In production, the proxy was not actually in front of the Node server. One line of Express middleware fixed it:

2. A hidden @import. A second font request appeared in the waterfall that I had never added to the page. It came from a scoped style block inside a “Buy me a coffee” button component, where someone (me, months ago) had written @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/...'). The bundler had merged that into the main stylesheet, so my entire CSS was waiting on a third-party server. I replaced that font with a system stack.

3. The headline was waiting for its animation. My hero used a fade-in with opacity: 0 at the start, 0.8 seconds long, with a stagger delay of up to 0.85 s. The browser cannot count an invisible element as the largest paint, so the largest contentful paint was literally behind an animation. I shortened it to 0.35 s with no stagger and a nearly-visible starting state.

With the real problems fixed, I went back to fonts and did it properly:

Accessibility also went from 95 to 100, after I raised the contrast of the footer text.

The score is a proxy. What I actually care about is that the page now appears in about a second and a half on a mid-range phone on a slow connection, and that I can explain why.
