#9694. November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Microsoft serves up an actively exploited Outlook zero-day, and a wave of critical Exchange, SharePoint, Windows Search, and LDAP bugs that exhausted defenders need to prioritize fast.

November offers up a veritable Patch Tuesday feast of vulnerabilities that are more likely to be exploited. In its second four-digit Patch Tuesday release in a row, Microsoft today addressed 1,093 security vulnerabilities, with 63 rated critical, and one zero-day in the mix (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS 6.5) that Microsoft confirmed is under active exploit.

"Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," says Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at Watchtowr.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out what actually matters when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention," he adds. "Our advice hasn't changed … start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what's already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

Related:OnlyFans Copyright Takedowns Expose Compromised Websites

To that end, security teams should prioritize CVE-2026-124194, and not just because attackers are already targeting it. It's a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook that may not allow code execution, hence its moderate severity rating, but could allow the disclosure of an account’s NTLMv2 hash — and in turn, the target's login.

"To exploit it, an attacker sends a target a malicious Office file and convinces them to open it," explained Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, in his monthly Patch Tuesday commentary. "If the attack succeeds, the attacker captures the victim's NT LAN Manager v2 (NTLMv2) hash, a value derived from their Windows password. The attacker may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password."

Security teams should also prioritize a pair of critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, in Exchange and SharePoint, respectively, that each open targets to any attacker with a low-privilege login.

The first, in Exchange Server (CVE-2026-118207, CVSS 8.8), "belongs in this week's emergency window for every Exchange Server Subscription Edition server you run," Automox researchers warned in their monthly Patch Tuesday bulletin, and "all an attacker needs to start is a low-level login."

It's an improper input validation that could allow an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send the server a specially crafted request and run code with no user interaction.

Related:The Evolving Cybersecurity Lexicon: Vulnerability Discovery to Resilience

"Code on an Exchange server reaches every mailbox it hosts," warned Automox researchers. "And Exchange usually holds broad rights in Active Directory, so the mailboxes are just the start."

Meanwhile, an important-rated flaw (CVE-2026-120002, CVSS 9.9) in SharePoint Server is an elevation of privilege vulnerability that needs quick addressing, according to Automox.

"The flaw is incorrect authorization," the researchers noted. "That 9.9 comes from a changed scope: a successful attack reaches past the vulnerable SharePoint component itself. An attacker who already holds a low-privileged account sends requests over the network and elevates their privileges, with no user interaction required."

Another critical RCE to watch out for, according to Automox, is CVE-2026-110043 (CVSS 8.8/10), a one-click heap-based buffer overflow in Outlook that uses the Preview Pane as an attack vector. A target must select a weaponized email so it displays in the Preview Pane for it to trigger the attacker's code, which runs with that user's permissions.

"Patch internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, and book the Exchange restart now," the Automox researchers advised. "Push the Office update this week, then check the installed build, because a fully patched Windows dashboard says nothing about Office. Rank by score and assessment, not label."

Related:Ivanti ICS Zero-Day Attacks Highlight Vendor Patching Hurdles

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero-Day Initiative (ZDI), also identified a Windows Search RCE (CVE-2026-116928, CVSS 9.8) as needing immediate attention.

"We start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server," he said in his November Patch Tuesday blog post, where he also listed 30 potentially wormable CVEs to patch quickly. "This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month."

And finally, Childs pointed to CVE-2026-119958, an RCE bug in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

"This patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction," he warned. "Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly."

Childs also recommended testing and deploying patches for the wormable bugs quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange.

White the cornucopia of CVE this month, especially on the heels of the record October Patch Tuesday, may feel overwhelming, security teams should stick to best practices and not get overwhelmed, advises Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra.

"I don't know about everyone else, but I'm tired," he said via email, adding that he believes that, eventually, AI will finish turning up old bugs and teams can once again look forward to smaller Patch Tuesday releases. "I can only imagine that if I’m tired, admins and operations teams everywhere are also tired. I believe that we will make it through to the other side, if we prioritize updates and focus on what really matters. The noise is coming at us from all sides, and we need to cut through it and figure out what really matters to the business."

Tara Seals is an award-winning journalist with 25+ years of experience as a reporter, analyst, and editor in the cybersecurity, communications, and technology spaces. As managing editor, she runs the newsroom at Dark Reading, leading a team of staff writers and freelance contributors. She also heads up strategy for a variety of in-depth, multichannel news coverage initiatives.

Prior to joining Dark Reading in 2022, Tara was editor-in-chief at cybersecurity stalwart Threatpost, and prior to that, the North American news lead for Infosecurity Magazine. She also spent 13 years working for other titles at Virgo Publishing (now part of Informa TechTarget), as executive editor and editor-in-chief at publications focused on communications service providers, channel partners, and enterprise mobile and video technology. In 2026, she was awarded a regional Azbee award for her in-depth coverage of the ongoing North Korean fake worker cyber campaign.

A Texas native, she holds a B.A. from Columbia University, lives in Western Massachusetts with her family, and is on a never-ending quest for good Mexican food in the Northeast.

#9693. Dev Tools Don't Need a Prettier Logo. They Need One Bold Branding Idea

Founder of Metabrand, a startup branding agency for AI, SaaS, and fintech companies.

Founder of Metabrand, a startup branding agency for AI, SaaS, and fintech companies.

Founder of Metabrand, a startup branding agency for AI, SaaS, and fintech companies.

Open almost any developer tool's website in 2026, and you will see the same branding. A dark background. A violet or green gradient. A terminal window with a blinking cursor. A headline that promises to make engineers ten times faster, and a logo that could belong to any of the other forty tools in the category.

None of this is bad design. It is safe branding. And for a developer tool, safe branding has a real cost: the people you sell to have learned to scroll past it.

Engineering leaders read a landing page the way they read a pull request. They look for the claim, then for the proof, and they discount everything else. "Powerful," "seamless," and "next-generation" are noise to them. So is a hero illustration of glowing nodes.

What they respond to is logic. Show them how the thing works, in their own terms, and they will fill in the rest. That changes what a brand is for. A consumer product can sell a mood. A developer tool has to sell an explanation you can see.

The fastest way to an ownable brand is to stop looking at other brands and look at the product. Every serious tool has a mechanic at its core: a data model, a workflow, a way of moving work from one state to the next. That mechanic is almost always more distinctive than anything a moodboard will give you.

The test is simple. If one sentence explains the product and the same sentence can drive the logo, the copy and the interface, you have a branding idea. If every surface needs its own metaphor, you have a style.

SuperPlane is an AI software factory built by the team behind Semaphore, the CI/CD platform. Agents take routine engineering tickets from issue to a review-ready pull request, and engineers step in only where judgment is needed. The company raised a $2.6M pre-seed round in June 2026.

The category problem was obvious from day one. Engineering leaders had seen every AI coding demo of the last two years. Another agent with another gradient would disappear.

The idea came from a line Elon Musk uses about companies: every person is a vector, and progress is their sum. We rewrote it for teams where agents do a growing share of the work. Every engineer and agent is a vector. Company progress is their sum.

A vector has length and direction. Agents add length: more work, done faster. Pointed in different directions, they cancel each other out and leave a mess in the codebase. SuperPlane sets the direction, so the work adds up.

That one sentence gave the brand one element to build everything on: the arrow.

The open-source engine behind SuperPlane has passed 8,000 stars on GitHub. A brand doesn't earn stars. But a brand that explains the product at a glance stays out of the way of the people who give them.

Before you commit to an identity for a developer tool, run it through the places where engineers actually meet your product:

If the idea survives all five, it will survive the market.

At seed stage, you don't need a mascot, a manifesto film or a 150-page guideline. You need one idea, a mark that comes from the product, a type and color system that works in dark mode, and a site that proves your main claim on the first screen. Everything else can grow from there.

This article was published under HackerNoon's Business Blogging program.

Founder of Metabrand, a startup branding agency for AI, SaaS, and fintech companies.

#9691. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9690. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

#9688. AI Training Environments That Evolve to Target Each Agent’s Weaknesses

Google develops search, advertising, cloud, and AI technologies at global scale.

Google develops search, advertising, cloud, and AI technologies at global scale.

Google develops search, advertising, cloud, and AI technologies at global scale.

Authors: Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, Rujun Han, Jun Yan, Yanfei Chen, Zoey CuiZhu, Ke Jiang, Peng Xia, Han Yu, Yufan Zhuang, Yifei Ming, Jiaqi Pan, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Jiaxin Huang, Burak Gokturk, Tomas Pfister, Chen-Yu Lee (Google)

LLM agents learn by interacting with environments, yet these environments are hand-built and static: blind to an agent’s weaknesses, and quickly left behind as it improves. While recent environment generation methods attempt to address this, they require domain-specific pipelines, rely on expensive or unreliable verifiers, and still produce static environments. To alleviate the engineering burden of rebuilding environments from scratch, we propose Environment Harness (EnvHarness), a programmable layer of plug-in components that wraps a static environment to reshape its behavior without modifying the underlying logic. Operating through standard interfaces, EnvHarness applies across diverse domains while ensuring every reshaped environment retains its original verifier. To automate this process, we introduce EnvRigger, which treats the target policy as a black box, observing its execution trajectories to synthesize EnvHarness components targeting diagnosed flaws, and validating them via fresh rollouts. Across five benchmarks in four domains, EnvHarness outperforms both original environments and domain-specific environment generation pipelines, achieving up to a 9.0-point improvement on held-out instances with 9.8% fewer execution steps. Furthermore, EnvHarness provides a superior optimization signal for reinforcement learning, enabling continuous, targeted co-evolution of the policy and its environment. github.com/google-research/envharness www.envharness.com

Figure 1: Overall performance. Left: Agents learning from EnvHarness environments consistently outperform those learning from the original environments across software engineering and office automation benchmarks, including SWE-bench Verified, OfficeQA, and SpreadsheetBench. Right: On SWE-bench Verified, under an identical environment budget, EnvHarness keeps improving as environments scale, while real and generated environments flatten out.

Figure 2: While an agent harness transforms a frozen LLM into a capable agent via plug-in components (e.g., skills, memory, tools) without altering model weights, EnvHarness applies this same principle to the other side of the interaction. It customizes a frozen environment with plug-in components while leaving original environment unchanged.

As LLMs are deployed as autonomous agents, the source of learning shifts from curated text data to interactive environments. Whether navigating web pages (Gur et al., 2024), resolving issues in a codebase (Yang et al., 2024), or controlling an embodied platform (Wang et al., 2023), agents rely on their respective environments to acquire learning signals (Yao et al., 2022b). These environments act as interactive counterparts that present specific tasks, manage changing states, respond to actions, and evaluate success (Li et al., 2026). Unfortunately, building them requires substantial human effort to hardcode the interaction logic and verifiers (Zhang et al., 2025; Merrill et al., 2026). Consequently, the resulting environments remain rigidly static, behaving identically regardless of which agent interacts with them or how much that agent has improved (Hu et al., 2026). This rigidity limits agent learning in two fundamental ways: it fails to provide a targeted signal that addresses a particular agent’s weaknesses (Dennis et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021), and it has nothing more to teach once the agent learns to solve the existing tasks (Wang et al., 2019; Beukman et al., 2024).

Since manually building environments is expensive, a growing line of work has turned to automated environment generation (Zala et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026). Despite its scalability, this approach suffers from two major limitations. First, generation pipelines are inherently domain-specific. Existing systems generate environments for web navigation (Trabucco et al., 2025), programming (Pan et al., 2024), or tool use (Lee et al., 2026a), but a pipeline built for one setting cannot transfer to the others. Second, ensuring correctness is both costly and unreliable. Because these environments and verifiers are generated by LLMs, practitioners must over-generate and heavily filter them (Wang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a), which still cannot fully guarantee their correctness.

Rather than creating new environments to obtain learning signals, we propose Environment Harness (EnvHarness), a programmable layer that transforms an existing, static environment into a dynamically customized one without modifying the environment itself. We make an analogy between EnvHarness and agent harness (Anthropic, 2025; Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026) in Figure 2: An agent harness provides LLMs with external memory, tools, and skills to handle complex tasks beyond basic text generation. EnvHarness extends this concept to environments, equipping a static environment with modular, plug-in components. A Stage sets the starting point of an episode, a Contract controls the allowed actions and observations, and a Chain connects multiple base environments to form an extended episode. The agent continues to use the standard interface, but EnvHarness mediates this interaction. This enables a single environment to fulfill needs it was never built for: isolating a specific skill, extending a task’s horizon, or calibrating difficulty so the agent struggles but ultimately succeeds. Crucially, operating strictly at the interface level makes EnvHarness domain-agnostic, while allowing every new environment to safely inherit the trusted, human-built verifier of its original environment.

While EnvHarness provides a universally applicable framework, its specific configuration must be tailored to each target policy and task. To automate this customization process, we introduce EnvRigger. By treating the policy strictly as a black box, EnvRigger observes both successful and failed execution trajectories within the base environment to diagnose specific behavioral vulnerabilities. Guided by these findings, it synthesizes candidate EnvHarness components and wraps the current environment to evaluate them. EnvRigger then runs fresh policy rollouts, judging acceptance solely on whether the candidate environment effectively cultivates the missing capabilities while remaining solvable. Components failing this evaluation undergo iterative revision until they succeed. Ultimately, this workflow realizes fully automated, task-policy-conditioned environment customization.

We conduct experiments on challenging benchmarks spanning embodied tasks (ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020)), web browsing (WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024)), software engineering (SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024)), and office work (OfficeQA (Databricks, 2025), SpreadsheetBench (Ma et al., 2024)). Specifically, we evaluate EnvHarness across two representative learning paradigms: skill-based learning (SL) and reinforcement learning (RL). In SL settings, agents trained with EnvHarness environments outperform those trained on original environments, achieving up to 9.0 points of improvement on held-out tasks (Table 2) while using 9.8% fewer interaction steps (Table 3). In RL settings, EnvHarness-customized environments similarly yield significantly stronger policies, with up to 6.5 points of improvement (Table 4). Finally, repeatedly executing the EnvRigger loop enables continuous co-evolution between the agent and its environment, unlocking compounding performance gains that scale effectively with the number of customized tasks.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) We propose EnvHarness, a programmable layer that customizes a static environment into a controllable one through its own reset/step interface, instantiated as three types of plug-in components that reshape environment initial states, agent-environment interaction interfaces, and composite tasks from different environments, all while the original environment’s tasks and verifiers stay unchanged. (2) We introduce EnvRigger to automate task-policy-conditioned environment customization. By diagnosing policy flaws from rollouts and iteratively revising candidate components until fresh rollouts confirm their success, EnvRigger ensures that every new environment targets the specific weaknesses of the policy. (3) Across five benchmarks in four domains, EnvHarness improves both effectiveness (up to 9.0 points on held-out tasks) and efficiency (9.8% fewer steps), strengthens policies under reinforcement learning, and scales agent performance where both human-built and generated environments flatten out.

Customization (states, rules, observations)

Table 1: Analogy between Agent Harness and EnvHarness. Both scale capabilities through external layers rather than changing the core system.

An agent harness (Anthropic, 2025; Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026) is the software layer (execution loops, tool registries, and context management) (Meng et al., 2026) that wraps a LLM to form an autonomous agent (Agent=Model+Harness). It adds new capabilities without changing the model weights. We apply the same idea to the other side of the agent-environment loop. We define EnvHarness as a programmable layer that wraps an existing, static environment and turns it into a customizable one (CustomizedEnv=StaticEnv+EnvHarness). EnvHarness achieves this customization by modifying the information flow through the standard interface, leaving the underlying environment completely untouched. Analogous to the tools and memory of an agent harness, EnvHarness is assembled from modular plug-in components that tailor the environment to specific training needs like isolating a specific skill, extending a task’s horizon, or adjusting task difficulty.

We model an environment as a tuple E=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},T,R,s_{0}), where \mathcal{S} is the state space, \mathcal{A} the action space, \mathcal{O} the observation space, T:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{S} the transition function that maps a state and an action to the next state, R the reward induced by the verifier, and s0 the initial state. An EnvHarness component is an environment-agnostic transformation w:

w reshapes the environment strictly at the interface level, without modifying its underlying simulator backend or implementation details. It customizes the initial state (s0′), filters exposed spaces (\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{O}^{\prime}), and updates transition mechanics (T′). Because all interventions remain external, the ground-truth evaluation logic is preserved, ensuring the original verifier still can score the episode.

Figure 3: Overview of EnvHarness components wrapping the standard environment interface. The underlying base environment (native state transitions and original task verifier) remains completely frozen. From left to right: the base environment, followed by three EnvHarness components—Stage, Contract, and Chain. Highlighted arrows and headers indicate overridden interface methods, with code blocks showing how each wrapper modifies state initialization, transition dynamics, or observation handling without altering the base environment.

The mapping w of Eq. (1) defines a general interface, and any transformation that follows this interface is a valid EnvHarness component. In this work, we introduce three concrete types of components, chosen to cover three fundamental modes of environment customization, and we expect more to follow. Each type is specified by its own parameters, overriding standard environment interface methods such as reset or step. Figure 3 compares the three component types with the original interface, highlighting the specific method each component overrides. We detail the software implementation of this interface protocol and class architecture in Appendix C. Throughout this subsection, we illustrate the components on one ALFWorld task, “put a clean mug on the desk”, where the default instance leaves the mug in the open and ends immediately upon placement.

A Stage, wstage,δ, is specified by a sequence of state-manipulation actions δ=(a1,…,ak). These actions are applied to the initial state s0 produced by reset():

Under this transformation, only the initial state changes. A Stage customizes the agent’s starting point, either introducing obstacles that require specific skills to tackle or completing early subgoals in advance to shorten the task horizon. For example, in our running task, one Stage executes the following sequence of actions: take mug 1, open drawer 1, put mug 1 in drawer 1, and close drawer 1 on the state returned by reset(). This Stage intentionally hides the mug from the agent, forcing the agent to face a more challenging scenario: search for the object first instead of directly reaching for it in plain sight. Conversely, another Stage can simplify the setup by executing cleaning the mug in advance, leaving only the final placement steps.

A Contract, wcontract,r, is specified by a triplet of transformation maps r=(fA,fT,fO), each defaulting to the identity. These maps rewrite the action space, transition dynamics, and observation space, respectively:

In practice, these transformations enforce action preconditions, augment or mask observations, and attach structured feedback to specific outcomes to steer agent learning. For example, on our running task, one Contract configures fO to truncate the room description after the first two sentences, requiring the agent to build its spatial representation across several steps; another Contract uses fT to block the clean mug action if the agent is not holding the mug, forcing the agent to pick up the object first; and a third Contract configures fA to remove high-level teleport navigation commands, forcing the agent to move and search step by step.

A Chain, wchain,ℓ, is specified by a pair ℓ=(Eext,g), where Eext is an additional environment and g is a composition logic. The composition logic combines the original environment E and Eext into a composite environment E′ exposed through the same interface:

To allow cross-environment combinations, the new spaces are simply the union of the base environments (e.g., \mathcal{A}^{\prime}=\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{ext}}), and R′ acts as the new composite reward. The composition logic g is unrestricted, allowing environments to be concatenated, interleaved, or branched dynamically based on intermediate outcomes (see Appendix D for examples). The composition logic g can either combine both environments from the start, or use the transition function T′ to dynamically transition from one environment to the next once a specific condition is satisfied. For our running environment, one Chain appends “heat a potato and put it on the countertop” in the same house, returning success under R′ only when both environments are verified. This requires the agent to learn to carry its goal past the point where it would otherwise have stopped.

Because all EnvHarness components share a standard interface, they compose freely. For example, stacking a Stage, a Contract, and a Chain on our base mug task yields a single composite environment:

In this setup, wstage,δ initializes the episode with the mug hidden in a drawer to enforce spatial search; wcontract,r truncates the observation to two sentences to evaluate partial observability; and wchain,ℓ appends a follow-up task to test goal persistence. Note that these transformations are non-commutative (w1∘w2≠w2∘w1); the nesting order determines how the resulting environment is constructed and which constraints apply during initialization versus active interaction.

Given a base environment E supporting a set of base tasks, and a target policy agent π, our objective is to automatically generate a modified environment E′ tailored to a specific task t, exposing the unique flaws of π to facilitate targeted policy improvement. A single EnvHarness component is itself policy-agnostic, as Eq. (1) defines w as a transformation of the environment alone, allowing the same component to be applied without modification to any policy. Conversely, the selection and parameterization of these components must be conditioned on both the base task t and the observed behavior of the policy π. We therefore introduce the task-policy-conditioned map \mathcal{H}:

where each wi is a customized EnvHarness component designed to wrap the base environment E and expose the critical weaknesses of π on task t. Rather than inspecting internal model weights, these components treat the agent as a black box and operate solely on its outputs to generate a steady, corrective training signal.

Figure 4: EnvRigger generating EnvHarness components for a target policy based on given task. The execution loop on the left runs the policy against the current environment, which is a frozen base environment wrapped by the active EnvHarness containing accepted components w1,…,wk, while the resulting rollout trajectories feed the EnvRigger loop on the right. The EnvRigger operates systematically through four distinct stages: Observe, Diagnose, Write, and Validate, where the last two steps form a write-and-validate loop that generates a candidate component, evaluates it on fresh rollouts, and revises it upon failure.

We introduce EnvRigger to realize the task-policy-conditioned map \mathcal{H} of Eq. (6). EnvRigger runs π in the environment on task t, analyzes the resulting trajectories, writes specific EnvHarness components to customize the environment for this task, and validates the customized environment using fresh policy rollouts. Candidates from customized environments that provide an appropriate learning signal are accepted, while the EnvHarness components of unsuccessful candidates are rejected or revised. Figure 4 illustrates this complete workflow, in which EnvRigger operates systematically through four distinct stages: Observe, Diagnose, Write, and Validate. To ensure that the initial state mutations introduced by Stage can be reliably reproduced, we assume the base environment supports deterministic resets during the validation phase.

The EnvRigger begins by running the policy π on the base task t in the current environment to collect and analyze a batch of rollout trajectories. While failures expose the specific weaknesses to be addressed within this task, successes help define the boundaries of these flaws, showing which capabilities are already intact and where they begin to fail.

EnvRigger analyzes the collected trajectories to identify the root causes of the observed behaviors, focusing on systemic issues such as repetitive action loops, failures in parsing long observations, or misread tool constraints. This diagnosis also determines the customization direction. For a struggling policy, the goal is to scaffold missing steps and simplify the task. Conversely, if the policy achieves a perfect success rate, it indicates the current environment is too forgiving to expose any remaining weaknesses. Under this scenario, the EnvRigger diagnoses that the environment must be made harder, shifting the customization to inject more challenging scenarios that force the policy’s potential flaws into the open. EnvRigger then outputs these findings as a textual diagnosis.

Based on the diagnosis, EnvRigger synthesizes one or more EnvHarness components to target the identified flaws. A single flaw may require combining multiple components, such as a Stage that customizes the initial state and a Contract that filters subsequent interactions, emitted together as a candidate set. For example, if the diagnosis reveals that the policy relies on a fragile shortcut that bypasses learning, EnvRigger can write a Contract that blocks this action under specific conditions, forcing the policy to explore and master the intended skills.

To evaluate the candidate components from the Write stage, EnvRigger wraps the current environment with them to instantiate E′ and runs fresh rollouts of π on the base task t. Based on some trajectory metrics, like the success rate and failure distribution, EnvRigger analyzes these fresh rollouts to decide between three validation behaviors: accepting the candidate, rejecting those that are unsolvable or non-challenging, or refining candidates with poorly scaled signals. If the candidate requires refinement, the trajectories and scaling feedback flow back into the Write stage, repeating this Write-and-Validate loop until a candidate is accepted or the revision budget is exhausted. All accepted components are ultimately added to the EnvHarness. The exact system prompt and decision-making criteria guiding these validation actions are detailed in Appendix A.

In this section, we mainly focus on the skill-based learning paradigm, where skills are extracted from environments to improve agent capabilities. We also evaluate the compatibility and performance of our framework under the online reinforcement learning paradigm, which is presented as part of our broader analysis in Section 5.

We evaluate our framework on five benchmarks spanning four distinct domains: ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020) for text-based embodied environments, WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) for web interaction, SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) for software engineering, and OfficeQA (Databricks, 2025) with SpreadsheetBench (Ma et al., 2024) for office automation. We report each benchmark’s native metrics, additionally tracking the average steps on SWE-bench Verified as a measure of execution efficiency. Training and evaluation episodes are strictly disjoint on every benchmark, with detailed split configurations provided in Appendix E.1.

Importantly, EnvRigger and the policy agent utilize the same model backbone on each benchmark: Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite for ALFWorld and WebArena, and Gemini-3.5-Flash elsewhere, ensuring that performance gains do not stem from distilling a stronger external model. On each training set, EnvRigger executes the optimization loop of Section 3 to generate EnvHarness-customized environments. We then extract skills from trajectories collected in these environments following ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2025), and evaluate the skill-equipped policy agent on the held-out instances. We exclude the Chain component from this automated pipeline because it is difficult for EnvRigger to observe the internal states of joined environments. Instead, we analyze the effect of chaining separately in Section 5.

We compare EnvHarness against four skill sources: No Skills (the frozen policy agent alone), Original Envs (skills from original environments to isolate reshaping effects), and GenEnv (Guo et al., 2025), VeriEnv (Chae et al., 2026), or SWE-smith (Yang et al., 2026a) for their respective benchmarks. While these baseline generators are domain-specific, EnvHarness applies generically across all domains via a unified interface, including the office automation environments where no generation baseline exists. To ensure a fair comparison, all baselines share the same seed instances, environment count, extraction pipeline, and policy model. EnvRigger operates strictly on training episodes under the same oracle verification access, and each evaluation instance is attempted once. Baseline details are in Appendix E.2.

Table 2 and Table 3 summarize the primary results across five benchmarks. Based on these evaluations, we present the following key observations.

Table 2: Performance of agents equipped with skills extracted from different environment sources on ALFWorld and WebArena. All numbers are the mean over three independent runs, with standard deviations as gray subscripts. Higher is better for every metric, and the last row reports the improvement of EnvHarness Envs over Original Envs. “–” denotes that the method is benchmark-specific and cannot be applied to the other domain.

Table 3: Performance of agents equipped with skills extracted from different environment sources on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeQA, and SpreadsheetBench. Standard deviations are gray subscripts. “–” denotes that the method is benchmark-specific and cannot be applied to the other domain.

Skills acquired in environments customized by EnvHarness consistently outperform those extracted from original environments on every benchmark, yielding up to a 9.0-point improvement on ALFWorld. Conversely, extracting skills from static base environments can actually degrade performance; for instance, on SpreadsheetBench, skills from unmodified environments fall below the no-skill baseline, while on SWE-bench Verified, they lengthen execution trajectories. Because static environments only allow the agent to practice behaviors it already executes, they fail to address its specific limitations, often retrieving redundant or suboptimal skills. In contrast, the write-and-validate loop of EnvRigger only commits environment components verified by fresh policy trajectories, ensuring that EnvHarness consistently improves upon the no-skill baseline across all benchmarks.

The underlying interface protocol, EnvRigger loop, and the skill extraction pipeline apply consistently across all five benchmarks, requiring only domain-specific prompt templates to adapt to different environments. By contrast, specialized generation baselines are constrained to their specific target benchmarks (indicated by dashes for inapplicable domains in Tables 2 and 3). Nevertheless, EnvHarness consistently outperforms these specialized baselines wherever they can be applied. On ALFWorld, EnvHarness skills surpass GenEnv by 5.7 points on average and by 8.5 points in out-of-distribution settings, where generic instance generation merely increases repetitive practice without addressing policy weaknesses. On SWE-bench Verified, EnvHarness outperforms the purpose-built SWE-smith by 2.46 points in success rate while requiring 5.11 fewer execution steps per episode. Targeting diagnosed vulnerabilities through a unified interface thus proves superior to merely scaling up the quantity of training episodes through domain-specific generation.

On SWE-bench Verified, skills extracted from EnvHarness-customized environments reduce the average steps per episode from 53.6 to 49.6, whereas skills from unmodified environments actually increase it to 55.0. This efficiency gain directly correlates with the specific diagnostics from EnvRigger: targeted Contracts and Stages designed to disrupt repetitive action loops and filter verbose observations successfully shorten execution trajectories.

We analyze EnvHarness along five dimensions: its compatibility as a training signal for reinforcement learning, its scaling efficiency compared to standard dataset expansion, its transferability across different policy model families and strengths, the unique value of the Chain component on long-horizon environments, and the capability of the EnvRigger to accept explicit, user-defined target constraints. Additional analyses are reported in Appendix G.

Table 4: Reinforcement learning on ALFWorld and WebShop, comparing policies trained on the original environments and on EnvHarness environments. ALFWorld is scored by success rate on in-distribution and held-out instance types; WebShop reports environment score and success rate.

Beyond skill-based learning, we investigate whether EnvHarness-customized environments can provide active training signals in online reinforcement learning. We perform this analysis on ALFWorld and WebShop (Yao et al., 2022a) using Qwen3-8B-base (Yang et al., 2025) as the policy, optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024); training details are provided in Appendix F.1. We train two distinct policies: one trained solely on the original static environments, and one trained entirely on environments reshaped by EnvHarness, evaluating both on the same held-out instances. Table 4 reports the results. Training on EnvHarness environments consistently improves policy performance, outperforming the baseline trained solely on original environments on three out of four metrics. Specifically, on ALFWorld, EnvHarness Envs achieves an in-distribution success rate of 87.9 compared to 81.4 for original environments. On WebShop, it achieves a higher score of 79.2 (versus 75.6) and success rate of 67.4 (versus 66.0). Although there is a slight, negligible trade-off in the ALFWorld OOD success rate (88.8 versus 89.6), the overall results underscore a fundamental advantage: the reshaped environments are not merely auxiliary data but provide a highly effective, independent optimization signal for online policy learning.

Table 5: Performance on long-horizon environments. SR stands for Success Rate, and AS represents Average Steps.

Real-world applications often require agents to operate over extended horizons. The Chain component addresses this by joining two randomly paired base environments into a single, extended episode. To isolate its effect, this pairing operates independently of the autonomous EnvRigger loop. We evaluate the extracted skills on standard single-environment test instances, reporting Success Rate (SR) and Average Steps (AS) in Table 5.

Skills from Chain environments yield substantial efficiency gains, reducing AS from 53.58 to 41.96. Their standalone SR (49.63) is marginally below the 49.88 baseline. This aligns with their stringent training condition—where success requires solving both halves—which prioritizes long-term goal preservation over short-task maximization. Combining both skill sets (Stage/Contract + Chain) achieves the best of both worlds: the highest SR (54.30) and excellent efficiency (43.12 AS), demonstrating highly complementary behaviors. Representative skills are in Appendix F.3.

Figure 5: Environment scaling on SWE-bench Verified. All three sources supply the same number of environments and feed the same extraction and retrieval protocol.

Environment scaling evaluates performance as the available training environments expand, comparing three allocation strategies under an identical budget: EnvHarness environments, unmodified benchmark environments, and SWE-smith generated environments. Holding the policy model, environment budget, and skill retrieval protocol fixed, each batch of 50 environments yields one skill bank (alternating between 2 and 3 skills per bank, totaling 15 skills at 300 environments). Crucially, while both baselines draw environment batches independently of the learner, EnvHarness synthesizes each batch specifically targeting the policy equipped with previously accumulated skills, enabling the environments and the policy to co-evolve. As shown in Figure 5, EnvHarness climbs from 47.67 to 54.79 (a 7.12-point gain) and maintains an upward trajectory at 300 environments. In contrast, the same budget yields only 52.13 on original environments and 50.37 on generated ones. This performance gap confirms that targeting the learner’s current capability boundary is fundamentally more effective than unconditioned environment scaling. Representative skills from each round are provided in Appendix F.2.

Figure 6: Cross-model results on SWE-bench Verified. Each group represents one policy model, ordered from weakest to strongest. Bars show success rates with no skills, with skills from unmodified environments, and with skills from EnvHarness environments. Percentages represent relative gains over original environments.

To evaluate generalizability, we test four distinct models on SWE-bench Verified: Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, Qwen3.6 27B (Qwen Team, 2026), Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026a). These span open-weight and proprietary architectures across a wide capability spectrum. In each setting, we use the same model backbone for both the target policy and the EnvRigger to keep the setup consistent, while the extraction pipeline and protocol remain unchanged.

Figure 6 shows the results. EnvHarness skills outperform real environment skills on all four policies, by 2.7 to 3.7 absolute points, even though the skill-free success rates span a broad range from 30.7 to 67.2. The size of this gain is largely independent of how strong the underlying policy is: the customization loop neither breaks down on the weakest model nor saturates on the strongest, and the same pipeline, prompts, and acceptance criteria are used throughout. What the policy’s capability level appears to change is the content of the diagnoses rather than the applicability of the loop. We note that skills of either kind help the two weakest policies most relative to no skills at all (+9.3 and +11.1 points for EnvHarness, and +6.1 and +7.4 for unmodified environments, versus under 5.5 points for the two strongest).

While the EnvRigger loop autonomously identifies training targets via behavioral diagnosis in standard settings, the same machinery can readily accept explicit, user-defined constraints. We evaluate two classes of constraints. The first is a quantitative target (success rate or average steps) for an objective performance metric in Appendix G. The second constraint targets capability weaknesses described in natural language. For example, given the weakness below, the EnvRigger generates a Contract that rejects code submissions unless tests are run. This forces the agent to verify its fixes. From the resulting trajectories, we distill the skill shown below. Rather than overfitting to a single task, the skill combines a general principle with actionable steps, perfectly matching our requirement for a skill (Yang et al., 2026b).

The policy submits a patch without running the failing test, so the fix stays unverified.

Description: Whenever a code change is made to fix a bug or implement a feature, especially where the test suite needs setup or configuration.Content: Before finalizing any change, run the relevant test suite to confirm the failure exists, then run it again after the patch to verify the fix, initializing the environment first when needed.

Environment scaling has emerged as a research direction that supplies agents with more environments to learn from (Huang et al., 2025b; Xi et al., 2025). Existing efforts scale environments in various forms, including simulating environments and their feedback with an LLM (Guo et al., 2025; Zala et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), up to world models that simulate or synthesize whole families of agentic environments (Zuo et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), synthesizing executable environments programmatically (Chae et al., 2026; Song et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026), and synthesizing new task instances inside an existing benchmark (Yang et al., 2026a; Pan et al., 2024). Beyond producing more tasks, another line adapts what the environment presents to the learner, from curriculum generation in reinforcement learning (Jiang et al., 2021; Dennis et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2026) to hand-designed corrective feedback and reward shaping (Lu et al., 2025). Different from previous works that rely on benchmark-specific pipelines or hand-designed curricula, EnvHarness reshapes an existing environment through one interface shared across benchmarks, conditions the reshaping on the diagnosed weaknesses of the current policy, and leaves tasks and verifiers untouched.

Self-evolving agents improve themselves from their own experience without additional human supervision (Fang et al., 2025). Existing efforts evolve different parts of the agent, including prompts and reflections (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023), skill and workflow libraries (Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026b; Xia et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026b), experience memory distilled from past trajectories (Zhao et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2025), the model weights through self-generated rewards or self-proposed tasks (Yuan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a), and recently the agent harness itself, rewritten and tested around a frozen model (Lee et al., 2026b). Different from these methods that evolve the agent while the world it learns from stays fixed, EnvHarness reshapes the environment itself against the diagnosed weaknesses of a frozen policy.

We introduce EnvHarness, a programmable layer that turns a static, existing environment into a controllable one. EnvHarness wraps a frozen benchmark with three plug-in components, Stage, Contract, and Chain, and reshapes it entirely through the standard reset/step interface, making it possible to isolate a skill, extend a task’s horizon, or calibrate difficulty in environments that were never built for any of these purposes. Since EnvHarness never touches internal code, a single implementation works seamlessly across different domains. Furthermore, by leaving the original tasks unchanged, every reshaped environment safely retains its trusted, human-built verifier. To fully automate this customization, we introduce EnvRigger, an autonomous loop that diagnoses policy weaknesses from execution trajectories and synthesizes targeted EnvHarness components to provide precise learning signals. This reframes environment construction as a wrapping problem rather than an authoring one, and suggests a practical pathway toward scalable environment supply for agent learning. We present future directions and limitations in Appendix I and Appendix H.
